category-accessories.heading: Blow molding accessories and conversion parts: blowing pins, stretch rods, mold shells, clamping bases and change parts, and when to replace them
category-accessories.intro: Blow molding accessories are the machine-side parts that hold, seal, stretch and transport the preform and the blow mold in a PET stretch blow molding machine, as opposed to the cavity that gives the bottle its shape. They are replaced for two reasons: wear during production, or a format change to a new bottle, preform or neck finish. This guide gives an overview of each part group, the signs that it needs replacement, and how to plan a spare parts or format change package for SIDEL, KRONES, KHS and other blowing machines.

sections.heading: Main groups of blow molding accessories and conversion parts
list: Blowing nozzles and blowing pins: seal on the preform neck and deliver pre-blow and high-pressure blowing air.
Stretch rods and stretch rod tips: push the heated preform down to the base before and during blowing, so the material is stretched lengthwise.
Mold shells (shell holders): carry the bottle cavity halves in the mold carrier and connect them to the cooling circuit.
Clamping bases (mold carrier bases): mount and locate the mold shells and base mold in the blowing station.
Change parts for bottle handling: star wheels, infeed and transfer guides and neck grippers that move preforms and bottles through the machine.
Cross-machine conversion parts: adapters that let one blow mold run on a different blowing machine.

sections.heading: Wear-related replacement: signs to watch in production
paragraphs: Accessories wear gradually, so a preventive maintenance plan that checks them at fixed intervals is cheaper than waiting for a stop. The signs below are typical across two-step stretch blow molding machines.
list: Rising air consumption or a hissing sound at the blowing station often points to worn seals or sealing surfaces on blowing nozzles and pins.
Bottles with an off-center injection point on the base usually indicate a bent stretch rod or a worn stretch rod tip.
A visible step or flash at the parting line, or bottles that vary between cavities, can come from worn clamping bases or mold shells that no longer locate the cavity halves precisely.
Uneven bottle temperature after blowing, or water traces around the mold, suggest a leak or blockage in the shell cooling connections.
Frequent transfer jams, fallen preforms or scuffed bottles point to worn star wheel pockets, guides or neck grippers.
Keep one set of the fastest-wearing parts in stock; LIHE's published lead time for replacement parts is 4 weeks.

sections.heading: Format change parts: new bottle, new preform, new neck finish
paragraphs: A format change is any change in the bottle or preform that the machine has to handle. Each type of change affects a different set of parts, and the parts are often delivered together with the new blow mold as one format change package.
list: New neck finish or preform: blowing nozzles or pins, neck grippers, preform infeed parts and, if the preform length changes, stretch rods.
New bottle shape or capacity, for example from 500ml to 1.5L: cavity halves or inserts, base mold, star wheels and guides sized to the new bottle diameter.
Hot-fill bottles, filled at about 85 to 95°C, need heat-set blow molds, because standard PET deforms above about 60°C; check whether the shells and cooling or heating connections suit the new mold.
Cross-machine conversion: when a bottle designed for one blowing machine must run on another, conversion parts adapt the mold to the second machine's carrier and blowing station.
Replacement and conversion parts are made from customers' existing parts or drawings for SIDEL, KRONES, KHS and other blow molding machines.

sections.heading: Mold shells and quick-change systems
paragraphs: With a shell system, the mold shells stay in the machine and only the lighter cavity inserts change between bottle formats. This follows the same idea as single-minute exchange of die (SMED): reduce the number of parts and adjustments that change during a changeover.
list: Shells are usually machined from lightweight aluminum alloy, which makes handling easier and conducts heat well.
New bottle formats can be supplied as cavity inserts only, if the shell system stays the same.
LIHE also builds split-type quick-change blow molds, and KHS InnoPET Blomax and Krones Contiform cold fill sets.
Check fit surfaces and cooling connections on the shells whenever inserts are changed, because a worn shell affects every format that runs in it.

sections.heading: How to plan a spare parts or format change package
steps: List the machine brand, model and number of blowing stations, and the bottle formats that run on it.
Decide whether the request is for wear replacement, a new format or a cross-machine conversion, because each needs a different set of parts.
Collect references for every part: original part numbers, drawings, or one used part per type as a sample.
For a new format, add the bottle and preform drawings and the neck finish so blowing pins, grippers and star wheels are made to match.
Send the list to sales@lihe-preform.com; parts for a new format can be delivered together with the blow mold to shorten the product launch.

faq.question: Can you make blowing pins and stretch rods for SIDEL, KRONES or KHS machines?
faq.answer: Yes. These parts are made from customers' existing parts or drawings for SIDEL, KRONES, KHS and other blow molding machines, and are matched to the preform neck finish.

faq.question: Do I need new mold shells for every new bottle?
faq.answer: Not if you use a shell system. The shells stay in the machine and only the cavity inserts and, if needed, the base mold change for the new bottle.

faq.question: How long does it take to get replacement accessories?
faq.answer: LIHE publishes a lead time of 4 weeks for replacement parts. For a new format, parts can be delivered together with the new blow mold.

faq.question: Which parts change when I switch to a new neck finish?
faq.answer: Typically the blowing nozzles or pins, the neck grippers and the preform infeed parts, and the stretch rods if the preform length changes. The preform mold itself also needs new neck rings.

faq.question: Can one blow mold run on two different blowing machines?
faq.answer: Yes, with cross-machine conversion parts that adapt the mold to the second machine's mold carrier and blowing station.

category-blow-mold.heading: PET blow mold overview: two-step vs one-step stretch blow molding, machine platforms and fill types
category-blow-mold.intro: A PET blow mold is the tool that gives a heated PET preform its final bottle shape: a stretch rod and compressed air expand the preform against the cavity formed by the mold shells and the base mold. This overview explains the two stretch blow molding processes, the machine platforms LIHE builds blow molds for, how cold fill, hot fill and aseptic filling change the mold, and how to choose the right mold set. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China.

sections.heading: How stretch blow molding turns a PET preform into a bottle
paragraphs: PET bottles are made in two stages of shaping. An injection mold first produces a preform, a small test-tube shape with the finished neck thread already molded. The blow mold then turns that preform into the bottle body. The preform is brought to a temperature above the glass transition of PET, placed in the closed blow mold, stretched lengthwise by a stretch rod and expanded sideways by compressed air until it touches the cavity walls.

Stretching in two directions orients the PET molecules, which gives the thin bottle wall its strength, clarity and gas barrier. The blow mold controls the final shape, the surface appearance and the cooling of the bottle, so the bottle design and the mold design are developed together.
list: Mold shells: the two halves that form the bottle body and shoulder.
Base mold: the separate bottom insert that forms the bottle base, for example a petaloid base for carbonated drinks or a flat base for still water.
Neck plate: the part that supports the preform neck so the finished thread is not deformed during blowing.
Conversion parts: adapters that let one bottle design run on different machines.

sections.heading: Two-step vs one-step (ISBM) blow molding compared
paragraphs: Blow molds are built for one of two process routes. In two-step (reheat) stretch blow molding, preforms are injection molded on one machine, stored and later reheated in an infrared oven on a separate blow molder. In one-step injection stretch blow molding (ISBM), the same machine injects the preform and blows it while the preform still holds heat from injection.

sections.heading: Blow mold machine platforms: SIDEL, KRONES, KHS, TECH-LONG, NEWAMSTAR, SIPA, ASB and AOKI
paragraphs: Every blow molder holds its molds in a machine-specific mold carrier, with its own clamping, locking, cooling connections and base mold movement. A blow mold must be machined to that interface, so the machine brand and model are the first piece of information a mold maker needs.
list: SIDEL: rotary two-step stretch blow molders widely used for water, CSD and sensitive beverages, including heat-set versions for hot fill.
KRONES: Contiform rotary two-step stretch blow molders, with manual and tool-free quick-change mold carriers on many models.
SIG/KHS: InnoPET Blomax rotary stretch blow molders, originally developed under the SIG brand and now built by KHS.
TECH-LONG and NEWAMSTAR: rotary two-step blow molders built in China and often installed as part of complete filling lines.
SIPA: one-step injection stretch blow molding systems that make the preform and the bottle on one machine.
ASB (Nissei ASB) and AOKI: one-step injection stretch blow molding machines used for beverage, food, cosmetic and pharmaceutical containers.

sections.heading: Cold fill, hot fill and aseptic blow molds

sections.heading: How to choose a PET blow mold
steps: Confirm the filling method and the actual filling temperature of the product: cold fill, hot fill or aseptic.
Identify the blow molding machine brand, model and mold carrier type, and whether the line is two-step or one-step.
Fix the bottle: capacity, target weight, neck finish, label area and base type, or send a sample bottle.
Match the preform to the bottle, or ask the mold maker to propose a preform that gives even wall thickness at the target weight.
Decide the scope: a complete set of mold shells, base molds and neck plates for every cavity, or a split-type quick-change mold with exchangeable inserts.
Plan the trial: blow sample bottles, check wall thickness, volume and top load, and approve the design before the full set is produced.

sections.heading: Bottle sizes, lightweighting and quick-change blow molds
list: Common water bottle molds cover 330ml, 500ml, 550ml and 1.5L formats; other capacities are built to the bottle drawing.

Lightweighting is done on both tools: preform lightweighting proposals reduce preform weight by 1g to 2g through neck or wall-thickness optimization, and the blow mold geometry is adjusted so the lighter preform still gives an even wall.
Split-type quick-change molds let a producer exchange only cavity inserts and base molds between formats instead of the whole mold set.
Beyond beverages, blow molds are built for edible oil, condiment, food, cosmetic, toiletry and pharmaceutical containers.
Published lead times: pilot molds 20 days, standard PET molds 8 weeks, replacement parts 4 weeks.
Finished parts are inspected on an in-house Zeiss CMM, and validation and inspection reports are available on request.

faq.question: What is the difference between a preform mold and a blow mold?
faq.answer: A preform mold is an injection mold that makes the preform, including the finished neck thread. A blow mold shapes the body and base of the bottle from that preform. In a two-step line the two tools run on different machines; in a one-step ISBM machine they work on the same machine.

faq.question: Can one blow mold run on different blow molding machines?
faq.answer: A bottle design can usually be transferred, but the mold shells, base molds and neck plates must fit each machine's mold carrier. LIHE supplies conversion parts so that one mold design can run on different machines, or builds a separate set for each platform.

faq.question: Do I need a hot fill mold for juice?
faq.answer: Only if the juice is filled hot. Products filled at about 85–95°C need a heat-set mold and a bottle with vacuum panels. If your line fills juice aseptically or cold, a cooled mold and a bottle designed for that method are used.

faq.question: Which is better for my plant, two-step or one-step blow molding?
faq.answer: Two-step lines suit high outputs and let you buy or store preforms separately. One-step ISBM machines suit smaller runs and special container shapes because the preform and bottle are made together. The choice is usually made when the line is bought; the blow mold then follows the installed machine.

faq.question: What information does LIHE need to quote a blow mold?
faq.answer: The machine brand and model, the filling method and temperature, a bottle drawing or sample with capacity and target weight, the preform and neck finish, and the number of cavities to be fitted. Send these to sales@lihe-preform.com.

category-closure-mold.heading: How to choose a closure mold: cap type, neck finish, cavitation and EU tethered caps
category-closure-mold.intro: A closure mold is a multi-cavity tool that forms plastic screw caps for bottles, either on a closure injection molding machine or on a SACMI compression line. This guide is a buying checklist: it explains the decisions that define a cap mold — one-piece or two-piece cap, neck finish, number of cavities, tamper-evident band and EU tethered cap design — and how each one depends on the product you fill. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China.

sections.heading: One-piece vs two-piece caps: the first closure mold decision
paragraphs: The cap construction decides how the sealing works and therefore how complex the mold is. Plastic caps are commonly made from polyethylene or polypropylene, and the choice of cap type usually comes before the choice of resin.
list: One-piece cap: shell, thread, sealing element (for example an inner bore seal) and tamper-evident band are molded in a single shot, usually in polyethylene. No liner is inserted, so the closure line is shorter.
Two-piece cap: a rigid shell, often polypropylene, plus a separate liner or sealing insert added after molding. Used where the seal needs a different material from the shell.

Mold impact: a one-piece cap puts all sealing geometry into the core, so core steel, polish and cooling matter most. A two-piece cap moves part of the sealing function to the liner, but the shell still needs accurate thread and band geometry.
Ask your closure supplier or brand owner which construction is specified before requesting a mold quotation; it changes core design, ejection and cycle.

sections.heading: Neck finishes for closure molds: 26mm, 28mm, 2925, 3025 and 38mm
paragraphs: The cap must match the bottle neck finish exactly: thread profile, thread start, sealing surface and the bead that holds the tamper-evident band. LIHE closure molds are built for 26mm, 28mm, 2925, 3025 and 38mm neck finishes, plus custom specifications.
list: 26mm: short, light neck finishes, typically used for still water.
28mm: the most widespread beverage size, used on finishes such as PCO 1881 and PCO 1810 for carbonated soft drinks and water.
2925 and 3025 (often written 29/25 and 30/25): short-height finishes used in lightweight bottle programs.
38mm: wider opening for juice, dairy-type drinks and other viscous or pulpy products.
If your preform is being changed to a lighter neck, the cap mold must change at the same time — supply the new neck drawing to both the preform and the closure mold maker.

sections.heading: Cavitation from 12 to 72 cavities: matching the cap mold to output
paragraphs: Cavitation is the number of caps formed per cycle. LIHE closure injection molds range from 12 to 72 cavities, and closure hot runner systems are available for up to 96 cavities. Higher cavitation raises output per machine but needs a larger clamp, a balanced hot runner and tighter cavity-to-cavity consistency.
list: Start from the required annual cap volume and the number of available production hours, then compare it with what one machine can deliver at each cavitation.
Check machine limits: clamp force, platen size, tie-bar distance, shot capacity and the ejection or unscrewing drive.
Lower cavitation (12–24 cavities) suits short runs, frequent color changes, larger 38mm caps and new designs still being validated.
Higher cavitation (48–72 cavities) suits high-volume 26mm and 28mm water and soft-drink caps on dedicated lines.
Plan for spare cavities: a mold that can run with individual cavities blocked keeps producing while a damaged core or cavity is repaired.

sections.heading: Tamper-evident band designs and EU tethered caps
paragraphs: A tamper-evident band shows the consumer that the bottle has not been opened: when the cap is first unscrewed, the band separates or stays on the neck. The band is either molded with its final shape or molded as a skirt and then slit and folded on a separate machine after molding.

Under Directive (EU) 2019/904 on single-use plastics, plastic caps and lids on single-use beverage containers of up to 3 litres placed on the EU market must remain attached to the container during use from 3 July 2024. This is usually achieved with a tethered cap: the band and the cap stay connected by a hinge or strip after opening.
list: Bridge-type band: thin bridges break on first opening; the band remains on the neck bead.
Folded band: an inward flap catches under the neck bead to make band separation reliable.
Tethered cap: a cut or molded pattern in the band leaves a hinge that keeps the cap attached and lets it be held open while drinking.
Tethered designs change the band geometry and often the slitting pattern, so confirm the target market (EU or not) before the mold is designed.

faq.question: What is the difference between a closure mold and a preform mold?
faq.answer: A preform mold forms the PET preform, including its neck finish, which is later blown into a bottle. A closure mold forms the cap that screws onto that neck finish. The two must be designed to the same neck drawing, so a neck change affects both molds.

faq.question: Do I need a new mold to make EU tethered caps?
faq.answer: Usually the band area changes: a tethered cap needs a band and hinge geometry that keeps the cap attached after opening, as required for beverage containers up to 3 litres by Directive (EU) 2019/904. Depending on the existing design, this can mean new cores, new cavity inserts or a new mold. Send the current cap and drawings so the change can be assessed.

faq.question: How many cavities should my cap mold have?
faq.answer: It depends on annual volume, cap size and machine. LIHE closure molds range from 12 to 72 cavities. Smaller cavitation suits larger caps and short runs; 48 to 72 cavities suits high-volume 26mm and 28mm water and soft-drink caps.

faq.question: Can one closure mold run both 2925 and 3025 caps?
faq.answer: No. Each neck finish has its own thread and sealing geometry, so the cores and cavities are specific to one finish. Some features, such as the mold base, can be shared when a conversion is planned, but the forming parts must be changed.

faq.question: Should my caps be injection molded or compression molded?
faq.answer: It depends mainly on the machines you run or plan to buy. LIHE builds closure injection molds for mainstream closure injection molding machines and compression molds for SACMI CCM lines; our separate article on compression vs injection molding compares the two processes.

category-compression-mold.heading: Continuous compression molding for caps: how a SACMI CCM line works and how to plan the tooling
category-compression-mold.intro: Continuous compression molding (CCM) is a cap-making process in which an extruder supplies a steady stream of molten plastic that is cut into single doses, dropped into open molds on a rotating carousel and pressed into finished closures. This page explains the process step by step, where it fits in a closure plant, which tooling a CCM line needs and how to plan a compression tooling project. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China.

sections.heading: What continuous compression molding is
paragraphs: Classic compression molding places a measured charge of material into a heated mold and closes the mold to shape it; it is widely used for thermoset and fiber-reinforced parts. Continuous compression molding for caps applies the same idea to thermoplastics such as polyethylene, but runs without stopping: instead of one press opening and closing, many individual molds travel around a carousel, and each one receives its own dose, closes, cools and opens in turn.

SACMI builds CCM (continuous compression molder) machines for plastic caps. Its CCM80, for example, carries 80 molds on the carousel. Because each mold works independently, a CCM line has no runner system and no shared injection shot.

sections.heading: How a SACMI CCM line works, station by station
steps: Extrusion: the resin is melted and conveyed by an extruder, which delivers a continuous flow of melt to the dosing area.
Dosing and cutting: a cutting device separates the melt into single doses of controlled weight, one per cap.
Insertion: each dose is placed into the open die (the cavity) of a mold as it passes the insertion station.
Compression: the punch closes into the die and the melt is pressed into the shape of the cap, including the thread and sealing features.
Cooling: the closed mold travels around the carousel while water-cooled tooling removes heat from the cap.
Extraction: the mold opens and the cap is removed from the punch and transferred out of the machine.
Downstream operations: depending on the cap, slitting and folding of the tamper-evident band, lining, inspection by vision systems and packing follow.

sections.heading: Where compression molding fits in a closure plant
list: High-volume beverage caps: water, carbonated soft drink, juice and tea caps produced in very large, stable quantities.
Lightweight caps: the dose weight is set per cap, which suits programs that aim to reduce cap weight.
Food and household caps: edible oil, condiment and cosmetic closures are also produced on compression lines.
One-piece and two-piece caps, tamper-evident bands and EU tethered caps, in 26mm, 28mm, 2925, 3025 and 38mm neck finishes.
Plants that already run SACMI CCM machines and need new cap designs, neck conversions or replacement tooling.
For the trade-offs between compression and injection molding, see our separate article comparing the two processes.

faq.question: Is continuous compression molding the same as classic compression molding?
faq.answer: It uses the same principle — a measured charge pressed into shape in a closed mold — but it is a continuous, rotary process for thermoplastic caps. Classic compression molding is mostly batch pressing of thermoset or fiber-reinforced parts.

faq.question: Does a CCM line need a hot runner?
faq.answer: No. Each dose is cut from the extruded melt and placed directly into its own mold, so there is no runner system. Temperature control is in the extruder and in the cooling of the tooling.

category-hot-runner-system.heading: Hot runner basics for PET preform molds: valve gate vs open gate, balanced manifold and AA control
category-hot-runner-system.intro: A hot runner is a heated system of manifold and nozzles inside an injection mold that keeps plastic molten all the way from the machine nozzle to each cavity gate, so no solid runner is produced and no material is wasted. For PET preforms and closures, the hot runner decides how evenly every cavity fills, how clean the gate is and how much acetaldehyde (AA) the melt picks up on its way. This guide explains these basics so buyers can compare hot runner designs. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China.

sections.heading: What a hot runner system does in a PET preform mold
paragraphs: In a cold runner mold, the channels that carry melt to the cavities freeze each cycle and are ejected as scrap. In a hot runner mold, those channels are heated and stay molten, so only the preforms are ejected. For high-cavitation PET molds this is standard practice: cold runners would waste resin and could not fill dozens of cavities evenly.
list: Sprue bushing — receives melt from the injection machine nozzle.
Manifold — a heated steel block with channels that split the melt flow to every nozzle.
Nozzles and nozzle tips — carry melt from the manifold to the gate of each cavity.
Valve pins and actuators — in valve gate systems, pins open and close each gate mechanically.
Heaters and thermocouples — heat each zone and measure its temperature.
Temperature controller — keeps every zone at its set point.
Backing plate and insulation — hold the manifold in place while limiting heat flow into the cooled mold plates.

sections.heading: Valve gate vs open gate hot runners compared
paragraphs: The gate is the small opening where melt enters the preform base. Hot runners use either a thermal (open) gate, which relies on temperature to freeze and reopen the gate, or a valve gate, where a pin closes the gate mechanically. Most PET preform molds use valve gates.

sections.heading: Why hot runner balance matters: preform weight and wall thickness
paragraphs: A hot runner is balanced when every cavity receives melt at the same pressure, temperature and time. If one cavity fills earlier or with hotter melt, its preform will be heavier or have a different wall thickness than the others. These differences show up later as bottles that blow differently, with uneven material distribution or weak spots.
With 96 or 144 cavities, even small differences between flow paths are repeated many times, so balance becomes the main hot runner design target.
list: Naturally (geometrically) balanced manifold — every flow path from sprue to gate has the same length, diameter and number of bends, so cavities fill evenly by design.
Uniform heating — each manifold section and nozzle is held at a stable temperature, so melt viscosity is the same at every gate.
Equal valve pin timing — all gates open and close together.
Check in production by weighing preforms from every cavity and comparing the spread, not only the average weight.

sections.heading: Acetaldehyde (AA) generation and melt residence time
paragraphs: Acetaldehyde is a by-product formed when PET is degraded by heat. Small amounts migrate from the bottle wall into the drink and can be noticed as a taste change, which is most critical for still water. For this reason, AA level is a common quality specification for water preforms.
The hot runner is one of the places where AA forms, because melt stays hot inside it until it is injected. AA generation increases with melt temperature, residence time and shear.
list: Small, streamlined melt channels reduce residence time and avoid dead spots where melt can stagnate.
Even heating avoids local hot spots that degrade the melt.
Moderate shear at gates and channel transitions limits extra heating of the melt.
Correct drying of PET before processing limits hydrolysis, which also reduces melt quality.

sections.heading: Temperature control: heaters, thermocouples and zones
list: Each heated zone has its own heater and thermocouple; large preform hot runners have many zones.
A failed heater or thermocouple causes one area to run hot or cold, which shows up as weight or gate problems in specific cavities.
Zone mapping — knowing which zone feeds which cavities — makes troubleshooting much faster.
Controllers should alarm on open circuits and deviations rather than silently holding output.

sections.heading: How to evaluate a hot runner for a PET preform or closure mold
steps: Define the application: preform or closure, cavitation, resin, and AA or gate quality requirements.
Confirm the injection machine (for example HUSKY, NETSTAL, KM or SIPA) and the controller and connector interface.
Review the manifold layout: is it naturally balanced, and how are flow paths and nozzle zones arranged?
Check the gate type and valve pin actuation, including how pins and seals are replaced.
Ask for the spare parts list (nozzle tips, valve pins, heaters, seals) and its lead time.
Agree acceptance tests: cavity-to-cavity weight spread, gate appearance and leak checks.
Confirm service: refurbishment options, remote troubleshooting and the written guarantee terms.

faq.question: Why do PET preform molds use valve gate hot runners?
faq.answer: A valve pin closes each gate mechanically, which gives a small, clean gate vestige and stable gate quality over long runs, and reduces drooling and stringing compared with thermal gates.

faq.question: What does a balanced manifold do?
faq.answer: It gives every cavity the same flow path, so melt arrives at the same pressure and temperature. The result is uniform preform weight and wall thickness across all cavities.

faq.question: How does the hot runner affect acetaldehyde in PET preforms?
faq.answer: AA forms when PET is held hot. A hot runner with short residence time, no dead spots and even heating limits AA generation in the melt.

faq.answer: Up to 144 cavities for PET preform molds and 96 cavities for closure molds.

faq.answer: Often yes, if the layout, pitch and cavitation match and the hot runner is in good condition. LIHE also refurbishes existing hot runners.

sections.heading: What machining capability means for a PET preform mold buyer

sections.heading: How machining affects tool life of PET preform and blow molds

Finishing after hardening: grinding and EDM after heat treatment keep final dimensions accurate despite heat-treatment distortion.

sections.heading: How machining affects interchangeability of conversion and replacement parts

Measurement: interchangeability is proven on a CMM, not by trial assembly.

category-mold-base.heading: Mold base for high-cavitation PET preform molds: flatness, parallelism, hole position and refurbished plates
category-mold-base.intro: A mold base is the assembly of steel plates, guide elements and connections that holds the cores, cavities, neck rings and hot runner of an injection or blow mold in exact position and connects them to the machine. In a high-cavitation PET preform mold the same plate carries dozens of identical stacks, so the geometry of the plates decides whether every cavity produces the same preform. This guide explains what the plates do, why flatness, parallelism and hole position matter, and when a refurbished plate is a sensible alternative to a new one.

sections.heading: What a mold base does in a PET preform mold
paragraphs: In a preform mold the mold base is divided into a hot half and a cold half. Each half is a stack of plates, and each plate has a clear job. The cavity components, cores and neck rings are the parts that touch the plastic; the mold base keeps them aligned with each other and with the machine during every cycle.
list: Hot half: the manifold plate and backing plate hold the hot runner manifold and nozzles, which feed melt to each cavity.
Cavity plate: holds the cavity inserts and gate inserts; nozzles from the hot runner seal against the gate area.
Core plate: carries the cores, which form the inside of the preform, and the cooling water supply for them.
Stripper plate and slides: carry the neck ring halves, which form the neck finish and open to release the preform.
Guide pins, bushings and locating elements: bring the two halves together in the same position every cycle.
Cooling channels: drilled through the plates to supply water to every cavity and core.

sections.heading: Why flatness, parallelism and hole position matter for high-cavitation molds
paragraphs: Geometric tolerances such as flatness, parallelism and position are defined on drawings using geometric dimensioning and tolerancing (GD&T). On a small mold a small error affects a few parts; on a 72-cavity or 160-cavity preform mold, the same error is repeated or accumulates across the whole plate.

head: Plate feature

sections.heading: Hole position and wall thickness: the link buyers notice in the bottle
paragraphs: A preform is blown into a bottle in a second step, so any variation in preform wall thickness shows up later as uneven bottle walls, weak spots or thin areas near the base. Wall thickness is set by the gap between core and cavity, and that gap is only uniform when the core and cavity bores are in the correct position relative to each other.
list: Hole positions in the cavity plate and core plate must match each other, not only the drawing, so both plates are measured against the same reference.
Hot runner nozzle positions must match the gate positions at operating temperature, because the manifold expands when it is heated; the design allows for this expansion.
Taper locks and neck ring locks help to center the stack, but they wear faster when the bores they rely on are out of position.
For molds built to withstand up to 8 million shots, as LIHE tooling on Husky, SACMI and Netstal platforms is, small position errors turn into wear over many cycles.

sections.heading: How to decide between a new and a refurbished mold base plate

Check the cooling channels for blockage or corrosion and the plates for cracks, especially around high-load areas.
Decide whether the mold layout will change (new neck finish, new cavitation, new preform); a changed layout usually needs new plates.
Compare the scope: plates that can be restored to drawing are refurbished, plates that cannot are replaced, and the whole mold is remeasured before it goes back into production.

faq.question: Is the mold base the same as the mold?
faq.answer: No. The mold base is the frame of plates, guides and connections. The cores, cavities, neck rings and gate inserts that form the preform are mounted in it, and the hot runner sits in the hot half.

faq.question: Why is plate accuracy more critical on a high-cavitation mold?
faq.answer: Because one plate carries many identical stacks. An error in flatness, parallelism or hole position is repeated across all cavities, causing differences in wall thickness, flash or wear between cavities.

faq.question: Can worn mold base plates be refurbished instead of replaced?
faq.answer: Often yes, if the plate is not cracked and the cooling channels are sound. Faces can be reground and bores repaired, followed by a CMM check. Cracked or heavily corroded plates are normally replaced.

faq.question: Do I need a new mold base for a neck finish conversion?
faq.answer: Not always. If the stack layout and cavitation stay the same, the existing plates can often be kept and only the neck rings and related parts are changed. A different cavitation or stack layout needs new plates.

faq.answer: Plates are measured on a coordinate-measuring machine (CMM). LIHE uses an in-house Zeiss CMM lab and supplies inspection reports on request.

category-preform-mold.heading: How to choose a PET preform mold: cavitation, neck finish, machine platform and preform weight
category-preform-mold.intro: A PET preform mold is an injection mold that forms test-tube-shaped polyethylene terephthalate preforms, which are later stretch blow molded into bottles and jars. This buyer's guide explains the four decisions that define a preform mold specification — cavitation, neck finish, machine platform and preform weight — and how they affect each other. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China.

sections.heading: Start from output: how cavitation and cycle time set preform volume
paragraphs: The output of a preform mold is simple arithmetic: number of cavities × shots per hour × productive hours. Cavitation is fixed when the mold is built, while cycle time depends on preform wall thickness, cooling design, resin, machine and post-mold cooling. For that reason, cycle time should come from your own production records or from the machine maker's data for a comparable preform, not from a general rule.

Choose cavitation by working backwards from demand rather than by picking the largest mold the machine can carry. A mold that is too large for the volume ties up capital and makes changeovers expensive; a mold that is too small forces overtime or a second machine.
list: Annual preform demand for each bottle size and neck finish.
Planned operating hours per year and realistic overall efficiency.
Number of SKUs (weights and colors) that will share the same mold.
Capacity of the downstream blow molders and filling lines.
Growth plan for the next 3–5 years, so the mold is not undersized on day one.

sections.heading: Neck finish families: PCO 1881, PCO 1810, 29/25, 38mm and wide mouth
paragraphs: The neck finish is the threaded top of the preform. It is not stretched during blow molding, so its dimensions and weight go straight into the bottle. The finish must match the closure and the capping equipment, so always work from the closure supplier's finish drawing and the relevant industry finish standard.
list: PCO 1810 — the earlier 28mm carbonated soft drink (CSD) finish with a taller neck; still in use on many established CSD lines.
PCO 1881 — a shorter 28mm CSD finish with less material in the neck than PCO 1810; switching requires matching closures and capper settings.
29/25 (2925), 30/25 (3025), 26/22 (2622), 25/22 (2522) and 1716 — short, lightweight finishes mainly used for still water and other non-carbonated drinks.
38mm — common for juice, dairy, isotonic and hot-fill bottles, usually with larger closures.
45mm, 68mm, 80mm and 90mm wide mouth — jars and containers for food and products that need a wide opening.
ROPP and custom finishes — roll-on pilfer-proof closures and finishes designed to a customer drawing.

sections.heading: Machine platform compatibility: Husky, Netstal, SACMI, SIPA and others
paragraphs: A preform mold is built for a specific injection machine. LIHE designs preform molds for HUSKY, NETSTAL, SACMI, SIPA, Milacron and other platforms, and its technical team can carry out an on-site machine interface audit before design starts. The points below must be confirmed for each machine:
list: Platen size, tie-bar spacing, mold height range and clamp force.
Shot size and screw capacity relative to total shot weight (cavities × preform weight).
Hot runner interface: nozzle position, heater zones, controller connectors and valve-gate actuation.
Ejection and stripper system, neck ring slide actuation and cam layout.
Cooling water connections, flow and temperature available at the mold.
Pitch and layout of the robot take-out plate and post-mold cooling tubes.

sections.heading: Preform weight and lightweight preform design
paragraphs: Preform weight is set by bottle volume, neck finish, wall thickness and the stretch ratio needed to reach the bottle shape. Resin is usually the largest running cost in preform production, so every gram removed matters over millions of preforms.

Weight can be removed in two places: the neck (by changing to a shorter finish, for example PCO 1810 to PCO 1881) or the body and base (by reducing wall thickness while keeping enough material for the required bottle performance). LIHE lightweighting proposals reduce preform weight by 1g to 2g through neck or wall-thickness optimization, and retrofitting an existing mold for lightweighting costs 25%–40% of a new mold price. Custom work also includes rPET material trials and special neck finishes such as PCO 1881 and 29/25.

Calculate annual demand and choose the cavitation from the required output and available machine hours.
Confirm the injection machine model and its interface data, ideally through a machine interface audit.

faq.question: How many cavities should my PET preform mold have?
faq.answer: Divide annual preform demand by the productive hours available, then by the expected shots per hour for that preform on your machine. The result gives the minimum cavitation; add margin for growth and downtime. LIHE builds molds from 2 to 160 cavities.

faq.question: Can one preform mold produce different preform weights?
faq.answer: Weight is set by the core and cavity geometry, so a different weight normally needs new cores, cavities or both. With the same neck finish, the rest of the mold can often be kept, which is the basis of a tooling conversion project.

faq.question: Should I choose PCO 1881 or PCO 1810 for a CSD bottle?

category-qc-equipment.heading: How to evaluate a PET mold supplier's QC capability: buyer's checklist for preform, blow and closure molds
category-qc-equipment.intro: A supplier's QC capability is its ability to measure, record and prove that every mold part and every sample preform or bottle meets the specification — not just the list of instruments it owns. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China. This checklist helps buyers assess any mold supplier's quality control: the questions to ask, the documents to request and the red flags to watch for.

sections.heading: Why QC capability decides mold performance on your line
paragraphs: Two PET preform molds can look identical on delivery and behave very differently in production. The difference usually comes from what was measured during manufacturing and how strictly deviations were corrected. A supplier with weak measurement cannot show you whether cavity 1 and cavity 96 are the same.
list: Uneven cavities lead to uneven preform weight and wall thickness, which shows up as blowing problems.
Unmeasured fits lead to early wear, flash and unplanned maintenance.
Spare parts without dimensional records may not interchange with the originals.
Claims without documents cannot be checked when a problem appears months later.

sections.heading: Questions to ask a mold supplier about quality control
list: Which instruments do you use, and are they in-house or outsourced? Ask specifically about a CMM, an optical projector or comparator, a 3D scanner and preform or bottle sample inspection.
Which parts are measured — every core, cavity and neck ring, or a sample from each batch?
At which stages do you measure: incoming steel, after machining, after heat treatment, after assembly, on sample parts?
What capability level do your critical dimensions reach, and can you show a Cpk calculation for repeated features?
How are instruments calibrated, and how often?
What happens when a part fails: rework, scrap, concession? Who decides?
Can you share a real anonymized inspection report before I place an order?

sections.heading: Documents to request before and after the order
list: Sample dimensional report: nominal, tolerance, measured value and deviation per feature, with part number and drawing revision.
Capability data: Cpk values for features that repeat across cavities. A Cpk of 1.33 corresponds to the process average being at least four standard deviations from the nearer limit.
Sample preform and bottle reports: weight in grams, wall thickness, neck finish dimensions and, for bottles, capacity.
Calibration records for the main measuring instruments.
Material certificates for mold steel.
Trial or approval report from mold start-up, if the supplier provides on-site start-up support.

sections.heading: Red flags in a mold supplier's QC
list: Only a final visual check, or only sample preforms measured, with no component measurement.
A CMM listed on the website but reports that only show hand-gauge readings.
Reports with all values exactly at nominal — real measurements always vary slightly.
No traceability between a report and a specific part number.
Refusal to share any example report, even anonymized.
Capability claims without a stated tolerance, sample size or calculation method.
No answer about calibration.

Measure some delivered parts yourself, or compare preform weight and wall thickness on your line, and check that they agree with the supplier's reports.

faq.answer: No. The CMM must be used on the right parts at the right stages, calibrated and documented. Ask for a real report and check that it is traceable to a part number.

faq.question: What Cpk should I ask for on PET mold parts?
faq.answer: 1.33 is a widely used minimum for capable processes; it means the average is at least four standard deviations from the nearer tolerance limit. Ask the supplier which features the value applies to and how it was calculated.

faq.question: Should I measure sample preforms myself?
faq.answer: Yes, where possible. Comparing your own preform weight and wall thickness results with the supplier's reports is the simplest way to confirm that their measurements are reliable.

sections.heading: How LIHE measures mold quality: CPK, defect rate and Zeiss CMM
paragraphs: Quality claims are only useful if you know what they measure. CPK, the process capability index, compares the distance between the process mean and the nearest tolerance limit with three standard deviations of the process. A CPK of 1.33 means the nearest limit is four standard deviations away from the mean, which leaves a margin for normal variation. A defect rate of 0.0064% equals about 64 defective parts per million. A coordinate measuring machine (CMM) probes the actual geometry of a part and compares it with the CAD model, which is how core, cavity and neck ring dimensions are verified.

sections.heading: Why in-house machining matters for PET preform mold precision
paragraphs: A multi-cavity PET preform mold is a stack of many small parts — cores, cavities, neck rings, gate inserts — that must fit together identically in every cavity. When those parts are machined in different workshops, each supplier works to its own process, fixtures and measuring habits, and the small differences add up in the assembled mold.
list: Tolerance stack-up: on a mold with 2 to 160 cavities, a small offset repeated across every core and cavity becomes uneven wall thickness in the preform.
Process sequence control: roughing, heat treatment, finishing, grinding and polishing happen in a planned order on one floor, so datums are not lost between suppliers.
Shorter correction loops: if a part is out of tolerance, it goes back to the same machine and programmer the same day instead of being shipped back and forth.
Predictable lead times: LIHE publishes 20 days for pilot molds, 8 weeks for standard PET molds and 4 weeks for replacement parts and cap mold parts.

sections.heading: Why in-house metrology closes the loop: Zeiss CMM and inspection
paragraphs: Machining only produces accuracy if someone can prove it. A coordinate-measuring machine (CMM) measures a part by probing points on its surfaces and comparing them with the CAD model or drawing. Having the CMM in the same building as the machines means measurement results feed straight back into machining corrections.
list: LIHE runs an in-house Zeiss CMM lab, and validation and inspection reports are supplied on request.

LIHE tooling consistently achieves CPK ≥ 1.33. Cpk compares the spread of a measured dimension with its tolerance; 1.33 means the process average sits at least four standard deviations from the nearer tolerance limit.

Other instruments complete the picture: a 3D profile scanner for contoured surfaces, an optical projector for two-dimensional profiles, and bottle sample inspection for the parts the mold actually produces.

page-machining.heading: Mold machining process chain: CNC milling, turning, grinding, EDM, engraving and polishing for PET mold parts
page-machining.intro: A machining process chain is the ordered set of cutting and finishing operations a mold part passes through, from a raw steel blank to a finished core, cavity, neck ring or blow mold cavity. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China. This guide explains what each process does, why no single process is enough, and which PET mold part needs which process.

sections.heading: Why a PET preform mold needs several machining processes
paragraphs: Each machining process is good at one kind of geometry and one stage of hardness. A round preform core is best produced by turning; a flat mold plate needs milling and grinding; a sharp internal corner in hardened steel can only be made by EDM. A mold maker plans a route through several processes so that each feature is made by the method that suits it.
list: Shape: round parts are turned, prismatic parts are milled, freeform surfaces are milled or engraved at high speed.
Hardness: most cutting is easier before heat treatment; grinding and EDM work on hardened steel.
Surface: functional surfaces in contact with PET need polishing; sealing and sliding surfaces need grinding.
Scale: a mold with up to 160 cavities repeats the same route on every core and cavity, so the route must be stable.

sections.heading: CNC milling on machining centers: mold plates, mold bases and blow mold shells
paragraphs: Milling removes material with a rotating multi-tooth cutter while the part or spindle moves along programmed axes. Multi-axis machining centers can reach several faces in one clamping, which keeps features in correct relation to each other.
list: Mold plates and mold bases: pockets, bores, cooling channels and bolt patterns. At LIHE, mold bases are machined on Mazak, Makino and Haas machines.
Blow mold shells and cavities: roughing and finishing of bottle contours.
Hot runner plates: manifold pockets and nozzle seats.
Fixtures and general parts that support machining and assembly.

sections.heading: Turning: cores, cavities and neck rings
paragraphs: Turning rotates the part against a stationary cutting tool and naturally produces round, concentric features. Most PET preform mold parts are bodies of revolution, so turning is the core process for them.
list: Preform cores: outside diameter and taper that define the inside of the preform.
Preform cavities: inside bore that defines the outside of the preform.
Neck rings: thread and neck finish profiles such as PCO 1881, 1716, 38mm or 45mm.
LIHE uses Hardinge precision turning centers for cores, cavities and neck rings.

sections.heading: Grinding: flatness, parallelism and fits on hardened steel
paragraphs: Grinding uses an abrasive wheel to remove small amounts of material with high accuracy, and it works on hardened steel. Surface grinding produces flat, parallel faces; it is the usual finishing step for plates and for faces that must seal or stack.
list: Mold plates: flat and parallel faces so that stack heights are equal across all cavities. LIHE grinds mold bases on Okamoto surface grinders.
Sealing and parting faces that must close without flash.
Fit diameters and shoulders on cores and inserts after heat treatment.

sections.heading: EDM and wire EDM: hardened details cutters cannot reach
paragraphs: Electrical discharge machining (EDM) removes metal with controlled electrical sparks between an electrode and the part. Because it does not depend on cutting force, it can make sharp internal corners, deep narrow slots and fine details in fully hardened steel. Wire EDM uses a thin wire as the electrode to cut through-profiles.
list: Gate inserts and hot runner details where small, precise openings control gate quality.
Neck ring details such as vents and thread features that a turning tool cannot finish.
Through-profiles and slots in inserts and plates, cut by wire EDM.
LIHE runs Sodick EDM equipment.

sections.heading: High-speed engraving and polishing: fine detail and surface finish
paragraphs: High-speed engraving machines use small tools at high spindle speeds to cut fine detail with small step-overs. Polishing then removes tool marks from surfaces that touch the plastic.
list: Blow mold cavities: embossed text, logos, grip patterns and fine radii on bottle shapes. LIHE uses Beijing Jingdiao high-speed engraving machines for fine details and polished blow mold cavities.
Preform cores and cavities: polished surfaces help the preform release cleanly and stay clear.
Neck rings and small inserts: deburring and edge finishing after machining.

Typical machining route for a preform core
steps: Saw and rough-turn the steel blank, leaving a finishing allowance on all functional diameters.
Drill or mill the internal cooling passage that carries water through the core.
Heat-treat the core to the hardness required for wear resistance.
Finish-turn and grind the functional diameters and fits on the hardened part.
Polish the surfaces that form the inside of the preform.
Measure the finished core on the Zeiss CMM and record the result against the drawing before assembly.

faq.question: Why not machine everything on one 5-axis machining center?
faq.answer: Milling is not the best method for every feature. Round parts are more accurate when turned, hardened flat faces need grinding, and sharp internal corners in hardened steel need EDM. A mixed route gives better accuracy and surface finish.

faq.question: Is EDM slower than milling?
faq.answer: Generally yes, so it is used for features that cutting tools cannot make or cannot make in hardened steel, such as gate details, narrow slots and sharp corners.

faq.question: Which process sets the preform wall thickness?
faq.answer: Mainly turning and grinding of the core outside diameter and the cavity bore, because the wall is the gap between them. Concentricity between core and cavity is verified on the CMM.

faq.question: Does polishing affect production?
faq.answer: Yes. Polished core and cavity surfaces help the preform release cleanly and avoid surface marks that become visible after blowing.

page-qc.heading: PET preform mold quality control workflow: inspection from steel to sample preforms and bottles
page-qc.intro: A mold inspection workflow is the sequence of measurements a mold maker carries out from raw material to finished mold, so that every stage is checked before the next one adds cost. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China. This guide walks through what is measured at each stage — incoming steel, machined components, assembly and sample preforms or bottles — and what an inspection report should contain.

sections.heading: What a PET mold inspection workflow covers
paragraphs: Quality control in mold making is not a single final check. A deviation found on a finished mold is expensive to fix, while the same deviation found on a single core before assembly costs one rework. A staged workflow therefore measures at four points.
list: Incoming material: is the steel the right grade and condition before machining starts?
Machined components: does each core, cavity, neck ring and insert match the drawing?
Assembly: do the parts fit together, align and interchange across all cavities?
Sample parts: do the preforms or bottles the mold produces meet the product specification?

sections.heading: Stage 1 — incoming steel and blanks
paragraphs: Mold steel determines wear resistance, polishability and corrosion behavior over the life of the mold. Common incoming checks in the industry are simple but prevent the most expensive kind of failure: a part machined perfectly from the wrong material.
list: Material certificate from the steel supplier compared with the grade on the drawing.
Hardness check of the blank, or of the part after heat treatment, against the specified range.
Visual and dimensional check of blank size so that the finishing allowance is sufficient.
Identification of each blank so that the part can be traced back to its material batch.

sections.heading: Stage 2 — machined mold components on the Zeiss CMM, scanner and projector
paragraphs: Component inspection is where most measuring time is spent. LIHE uses an in-house Zeiss CMM lab, a 3D profile scanner and an optical projector at this stage. Features are measured against the CAD model and the drawing tolerances.
list: Cores and cavities: diameters, lengths, concentricity and the geometry that sets preform wall thickness — measured on the CMM.
Neck rings: thread and neck finish profiles such as PCO 1881 or 29/25 — measured on the CMM and checked as a two-dimensional profile on the optical projector.
Gate inserts and hot runner parts: small bores and seats that control gate quality and sealing — measured on the CMM.
Mold plates and mold base: flatness, hole positions and parallelism that keep up to 160 cavities aligned.
Blow mold cavities: freeform bottle contours compared with the 3D model on the 3D profile scanner.

sections.heading: Stage 3 — assembly, fit and interchangeability checks
paragraphs: Individually correct parts can still assemble badly if fits, stack heights or alignment features do not work together. Assembly checks confirm that the mold behaves as one unit.
list: Stack fit: each core, cavity and neck ring set closes and aligns without forcing.
Interchangeability: parts from one cavity fit any other cavity. LIHE supplies 100% interchangeable conversion parts for Husky, SACMI, SIPA, NETSTAL, MHT, OTTO, ASB, Krupps and Corvaglia systems.
Cooling circuits: water channels are open and correctly connected so that every cavity cools evenly.
Moving and sealing surfaces: clearances are checked so that the mold can run up to 8 million shots on Husky, SACMI and Netstal platforms.

sections.heading: Stage 4 — sample preform and bottle inspection
paragraphs: The final proof of a mold is the part it makes. LIHE's QC equipment includes dedicated bottle sample inspection for this stage. Typical checks on sample preforms and bottles include:
list: Preform weight in grams, which matters when a lightweighting project removes 1g to 2g from a design.
Wall thickness and its uniformity around the circumference, which affects blowing.
Neck finish dimensions, so that the closure seals on the filling line.
Overall length and visual defects such as gate marks or flash.
For blow molds: bottle dimensions, wall thickness distribution and capacity, for example on 330ml, 500ml or 1.5L water bottles.

sections.heading: What the inspection report should contain
paragraphs: LIHE supplies validation and inspection reports on request. A useful dimensional report is traceable and lets a buyer compare measured values with tolerances without guessing.
list: Part identification, drawing number and revision.
Nominal value, tolerance, measured value and deviation for each feature.
Pass or fail status, instrument used and date of measurement.
For repeated features across many cavities, capability statistics. LIHE tooling consistently achieves CPK ≥ 1.33.

sections.heading: How to request and review inspection reports
steps: State in the purchase order which parts need dimensional reports — for example all cores, cavities and neck rings of a new preform mold.
List the critical features that matter to your line, such as neck finish, preform weight or a specific Husky or SACMI interface.
When the reports arrive, check that each part number matches the parts in the shipment.
Compare measured values against tolerances and look at how centered they are, not only whether they pass.
Keep the reports as a baseline, so that worn parts can later be compared with their original dimensions during maintenance or replacement.

faq.question: Which stages of mold production does LIHE inspect?
faq.answer: LIHE's QC equipment — Zeiss CMM, 3D profile scanner, optical projector and bottle sample inspection — covers machined components and the sample preforms and bottles a mold produces. Validation and inspection reports are supplied on request.

faq.question: Why measure components before assembly instead of only testing the finished mold?
faq.answer: A deviation found on a single core costs one rework. The same deviation found after assembly may require taking the mold apart and delaying shipment, so staged inspection protects the lead time.

faq.question: What is checked on sample preforms?
faq.answer: Typically weight in grams, wall thickness and its uniformity, neck finish dimensions, length and visual defects such as gate marks or flash.

faq.question: What does CPK ≥ 1.33 tell me in an inspection report?
faq.answer: It shows that a dimension repeated across parts is both centered and consistent: the process average is at least four standard deviations from the nearer tolerance limit. LIHE tooling consistently achieves this level.

faq.question: Can I use the inspection report later for spare parts?
faq.answer: Yes. The original measured values are a useful baseline when comparing worn parts, and they support ordering replacement parts, which LIHE supplies with a 4-week lead time.

product-17.heading: Machining equipment reference for PET preform and blow molds: Mazak, Makino, Okamoto, Haas, Hardinge, Beijing Jingdiao and Sodick
product-17.intro: Machining equipment in mold making refers to the CNC machine tools — machining centers, turning centers, grinders, engraving machines and EDM machines — that shape steel into mold plates, cores, cavities, neck rings and blow mold cavities. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China. This page is a brand-by-brand reference: what each machine builder is known for and what its machines do in PET mold making.

sections.heading: Why the machine brand matters in PET preform mold making
paragraphs: Machine tool builders specialize. Some focus on rigid multi-axis machining centers, some on precision turning, some on grinding or EDM. A buyer who knows what each brand is built for can judge whether a mold maker has the right machine for each part — not just a long list of machines.
list: Accuracy and repeatability: a machine's spindle, guideways and thermal behavior set how closely it holds size over a long batch of identical parts.
Specialization: turning, milling, grinding and EDM each need a dedicated machine type to reach their best results.
Consistency: a mold with up to 160 cavities needs the same part machined many times with the same result.
Limits: a brand is not a guarantee by itself — programming, tooling, fixturing and measurement decide the final result.

sections.heading: Mazak and Makino (Japan): machining centers for mold plates, cavities and blow mold shells
paragraphs: Yamazaki Mazak is a Japanese builder of machining centers, turning centers and multi-tasking machines that combine turning and milling. Makino, also from Japan, is known for machining centers and EDM machines aimed at die and mold work, including high-speed machining of hardened steel.
list: Mold making role: multi-axis milling of mold plates and mold bases, cavity pockets, cooling channels and blow mold shells.
Why multi-axis matters: machining several faces in one clamping keeps bores, pockets and faces in correct relation to each other.
Why high-speed machining matters: small tools at high spindle speeds produce accurate contours and good surface finish on blow mold cavities, reducing polishing time.
At LIHE, mold bases are machined on Mazak, Makino and Haas machines.

sections.heading: Okamoto (Japan): precision surface grinding of plates and components
paragraphs: Okamoto is a Japanese builder of grinding machines, including surface grinders. Grinding works on hardened steel and produces flat, parallel faces with fine finish.
list: Mold making role: finishing mold plates and components to flatness and parallelism after heat treatment.
Why it matters: equal stack heights across all cavities depend on plates being flat and parallel; sealing faces must close without flash.
At LIHE, mold bases are ground on Okamoto machines and then verified on the Zeiss CMM.

sections.heading: Haas and Hardinge (USA): general CNC machining and precision turning
paragraphs: Haas Automation, based in California, builds CNC vertical and horizontal machining centers and lathes that are widely used for general machining. Hardinge, based in New York State, is known for precision lathes and turning centers designed for close-tolerance round parts.
list: Haas mold making role: general milling of plates, fixtures and supporting parts, and capacity for mold base machining.
Hardinge mold making role: turning of preform cores, cavities and neck rings — round parts where diameter and concentricity set preform wall thickness.
Why precision turning matters: turned features are naturally concentric, which is what core-to-cavity alignment needs.

sections.heading: Beijing Jingdiao (China): high-speed engraving for fine detail
paragraphs: Beijing Jingdiao builds high-speed precision machining and engraving centers designed for small tools, fine features and high surface quality.
list: Mold making role: embossed text, logos, grip patterns and fine radii in blow mold cavities, and small precise features on inserts.
Why it matters: fine detail cut accurately needs less hand finishing, which keeps cavities consistent across a multi-cavity blow mold set.
At LIHE, Jingdiao machines are used for fine details and polished blow mold cavities.

sections.heading: Sodick (Japan): EDM and wire EDM for hardened details
paragraphs: Sodick is a Japanese builder of electrical discharge machines, including die-sinking EDM and wire EDM. EDM removes metal with electrical sparks, so it can cut fully hardened steel and produce sharp internal corners and narrow slots that cutting tools cannot reach.
list: Mold making role: gate inserts, hot runner details, neck ring vents and thread details, and through-profiles in inserts and plates.
Why it matters: gate details control gate quality on every preform; making them after hardening avoids distortion from heat treatment.

product-18.heading: QC equipment reference for PET preform and blow molds: Zeiss CMM, 3D profile scanner, optical projector and bottle inspection
product-18.intro: QC equipment in mold making refers to the measuring instruments used to verify that mold components and the parts they produce match the drawing and the CAD model. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China. This page is an instrument-by-instrument reference: how each instrument in LIHE's QC lab works, which features it is suited to, and where its limits are.

sections.heading: Zeiss CMM: three-dimensional measurement of cores, cavities and plates
paragraphs: A coordinate-measuring machine (CMM) moves a probe along three perpendicular axes and records the X, Y and Z position of each point it touches. Software fits these points to geometric elements — circles, cylinders, cones, planes — and compares them with nominal values. LIHE runs an in-house Zeiss CMM lab.
list: How it measures: the part is aligned to its datums, then the probe touches or scans the surface. Results are reported in millimeters, usually to the micron level.
Typical features on PET mold parts: core and cavity diameters, taper, concentricity between features, stack lengths, bore positions on plates and the geometry of gate seats.
Why it matters: the preform wall is the gap between core and cavity, so their relationship in three dimensions has to be measured, not assumed. LIHE mold bases are also verified on the Zeiss CMM.
Limits: contact measurement takes time per point, and results depend on stable temperature, correct fixturing and a calibrated probe.

sections.heading: 3D profile scanner: freeform surfaces of blow mold cavities
paragraphs: A 3D profile scanner captures a dense cloud of surface points without touching the part, typically by projecting light patterns or laser lines and recording them with cameras. The point cloud is aligned to the CAD model, and deviations are shown as a color map across the whole surface.
list: Typical features: bottle contours, shoulder and base shapes, grip panels, embossed text and logos in blow mold cavities, and other complex shapes.
Why it matters: a bottle shape cannot be described by a few diameters; a full-surface comparison shows local deviations that point measurements would miss.
Output: a deviation color map and section profiles compared with the 3D model.
Limits: for tight fit diameters a CMM is usually the more precise choice, and highly polished surfaces can be harder to capture optically.

sections.heading: Optical projector: two-dimensional profiles of neck finishes and small features
paragraphs: An optical projector, also called an optical comparator, projects a magnified silhouette of a part onto a screen. The operator compares the outline with an overlay drawing or measures distances and angles directly on the screen. It measures without contact and is fast for profiles.
list: Typical features: thread profiles and neck finish outlines on neck rings, small radii, chamfers, edges and step heights.
Why it matters: neck finishes such as PCO 1881, PCO 1810, 1716, 3025 or 2925 must match the closure; a magnified outline shows thread form errors clearly.
Output: dimensions and a pass or fail comparison with the profile drawing.
Limits: it sees only the silhouette in one plane, so three-dimensional relationships still need the CMM.

sections.heading: Bottle and preform sample inspection: checking what the mold produces
paragraphs: Instruments that measure steel parts cannot confirm how the mold behaves in production. LIHE's QC equipment therefore includes dedicated bottle sample inspection, which measures sample preforms and bottles.
list: Preform checks: weight in grams, wall thickness and its uniformity around the circumference, neck finish dimensions and length.
Bottle checks: overall dimensions, wall thickness distribution from neck to base, and capacity — for example on 330ml, 500ml, 550ml or 1.5L water bottles.
Why it matters: uneven preform walls cause uneven stretching in blowing; bottle walls that are too thin can fail, especially in hot fill at about 85–95°C.
Limits: sample results describe the samples tested, so the number of samples per cavity should be agreed for multi-cavity molds.

faq.question: Why use both a CMM and an optical projector on a neck ring?
faq.answer: The CMM measures three-dimensional relationships such as concentricity and position, while the optical projector shows the magnified thread and neck finish outline in one plane. Together they cover both fit and profile.

faq.question: Is a 3D scanner more accurate than a CMM?
faq.answer: Not for fit diameters. A scanner is faster at capturing whole freeform surfaces such as blow mold cavities; a tactile CMM is generally the better choice for tight tolerances on cores, cavities and plates.

faq.question: What does bottle sample inspection add if the mold parts already passed?
faq.answer: It checks the result of the whole system — mold, cooling and process — on real preforms and bottles: weight, wall thickness, neck dimensions and capacity.

faq.question: Can I receive measurement data with my mold or spare parts?
faq.answer: Yes. LIHE supplies validation and inspection reports with molds and spare parts on request.

faq.question: Why does temperature matter for CMM measurement?
faq.answer: Steel expands as it warms, so a part measured at a different temperature reads a different size. Stable temperature in the measuring room keeps CMM results comparable.

product-19.heading: PET preform mold technical reference: mold stack, cooling, venting, wear parts and maintenance
product-19.intro: A PET preform mold stack is the set of precision components — core, cavity, neck ring, gate insert and lock ring — that together form one preform in each cavity of the mold. This reference explains what each stack component does, how cooling and venting affect preform quality, which parts wear, how maintenance is usually planned and what to include when ordering a mold or spare stack parts. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a PET preform mold stack
paragraphs: A multi-cavity preform mold repeats the same stack in every cavity, from 2 up to 160 cavities in LIHE molds. The stacks sit between the core plate, stripper plate, cavity plate and the hot runner. Every stack part must be interchangeable between cavities so that a worn part can be replaced without rework.
list: Core — forms the inside of the preform. It is cooled from the inside by a central cooling tube and its length and diameter set the preform's inner shape.
Cavity — forms the outside of the preform body. It is surrounded by cooling channels and determines the outer diameter and wall thickness together with the core.
Neck ring (thread splits) — two halves that form the neck finish and support ring. They open sideways on slides to release the threads and then push the preform off the core.
Gate insert — forms the preform base and the gate area where the hot runner nozzle injects melt. It needs strong cooling because the gate is the last area to freeze.

Lock ring and tapers — the cavity lock ring holds the cavity and gate insert in the cavity plate; matching tapers on core, neck ring and cavity align the stack so the core is concentric with the cavity.
Core lock ring / stripper parts — locate the neck ring on the core side and transfer the ejection movement.

sections.heading: Cooling layout and its effect on cycle time
paragraphs: In most preform molds the cooling time is the largest part of the cycle, so cooling design decides how fast the mold can run. Heat has to be removed evenly from core, cavity, neck and gate; if one area stays hot, the whole cycle has to wait for it, or the preform will show defects such as ovality, gate crystallinity or sticking.

LIHE optimizes cooling as part of its design work; optimized cooling can reduce neck cooling time by up to 0.5 seconds. Detailed cycle times depend on the preform and machine and are not quoted as general figures.
list: Core cooling: a bubbler or cooling tube delivers water to the tip of the core and returns it along the core wall.
Cavity cooling: annular or spiral channels around the cavity, sealed with O-rings.
Gate cooling: dedicated channels in the gate insert, critical for a clean, clear gate area.
Neck ring cooling: channels in the neck ring halves; the thick neck finish is often a limiting area.
Water quality: scale and corrosion inside channels reduce heat transfer, so treated, filtered water and regular flow checks protect cycle time.

sections.heading: Venting in preform molds
paragraphs: As melt fills a cavity, the air inside must escape through very shallow vents, mainly at the neck ring split line and at the top of the neck finish. Vents are shallow enough to let air out but not plastic.

Blocked vents trap air, which can cause short shots on the thread, burn marks or incomplete support rings. Vents slowly fill with residue during production, so vent cleaning is one of the most frequent maintenance tasks on a preform mold.

sections.heading: Preventive maintenance planning for a preform mold
paragraphs: Preform mold maintenance is normally planned by shot count, not by calendar time, because wear depends on how many cycles the mold has run. Exact intervals depend on the preform, resin, machine and the mold maker's manual. LIHE molds are built to withstand up to 8 million shots on Husky/SACMI/Netstal platforms, and LIHE's technical team provides regular preventive maintenance and mold refurbishment programs.

At planned short stops: clean vents and parting surfaces, check neck ring slides and ejection movement.
At scheduled stack services: dismantle stacks, measure tapers and critical diameters, replace O-rings, descale cooling channels.
At major overhauls: refurbish or replace worn cores, cavities and neck rings and verify alignment of the full mold.
Record every action against the shot counter so wear trends can be seen early.

faq.answer: Neck rings and their vents usually need attention first because they slide, open and close every cycle and carry the thread detail. Seals and O-rings in the cooling circuits are also replaced at every stack service.

faq.answer: Cooling is usually the longest part of the cycle. Even cooling of core, cavity, neck and gate lets the mold run faster without defects. LIHE's optimized cooling can reduce neck cooling time by up to 0.5 seconds.
