product-20.heading: Closure mold technical reference: core and cavity, ejection, hot runner, cooling and wear parts
product-20.intro: A closure injection mold is a multi-cavity tool in which molten plastic is injected through a hot runner into cap-shaped cavities, cooled against steel cores and then ejected as finished screw caps. This page is a technical reference for engineers who run or buy cap molds: how the forming parts are arranged, how threaded caps are released from the core, what the hot runner and cooling circuits do, which parts wear and what to send when ordering. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China.

sections.heading: Closure mold anatomy: core, cavity and mold base
paragraphs: Every cavity of a cap mold is a small set of precision inserts mounted in a common mold base. The cavity side forms the outside of the cap (top panel, knurling or grip ribs, skirt); the core side forms the inside (thread, inner seal, tamper-evident band). Because the thread and seal are on the core, most of the dimensional risk in a closure mold sits on the core side.
list: Cavity insert: forms the outer shell and top panel; its surface finish defines cap appearance and printability.
Core insert and inner core: form the thread, the inner bore seal or olive seal and the band geometry.
Stripper ring or sleeve: pushes the cap off the core at ejection and forms the lower edge of the skirt or band.
Mold base: plates, guide pillars and taper locks that hold every cavity in alignment so that cap walls stay even.
Hot runner half: manifold and nozzles that deliver melt to each gate at the top center of the cap.
Cooling circuits: channels in cavity plates and bubblers or baffles inside each core.

sections.heading: Unscrewing vs stripping ejection for threaded caps
paragraphs: A screw cap has an internal thread, which is an undercut: the cap cannot simply be pushed straight off a rigid core without either rotating it or flexing it. Closure molds solve this in two general ways. Which one fits depends on the thread profile, the resin and the band design, and it is decided together with the cap design.

Stripping (bump-off) ejection

A stripper ring pushes the cap off the core; the cap skirt flexes elastically over the thread
Rack and gear, hydraulic or electric motor drive in the mold
Ejector stroke of the machine or mold; no rotating parts
Deep, sharp or long threads; rigid resins

sections.heading: Closure hot runner systems up to 96 cavities
paragraphs: In a multi-cavity cap mold, the hot runner keeps the plastic molten from the machine nozzle to each gate, so no cold runner is produced and every cavity fills at the same time. LIHE supplies closure hot runner systems of up to 96 cavities; LIHE hot runners use a Husky Ultra-type design with a 3-year leakage-proof guarantee.
list: Balance: the manifold layout gives every cavity the same flow length so cap weights stay consistent across the mold.
Gate type: valve gates close mechanically and leave a clean gate mark on the cap top panel; this is important for printed or visible top panels.
Temperature zones: each nozzle has its own heater and thermocouple, so a cold or overheated zone shows as a short or heavy cap in that cavity.
Service parts: nozzle tips, valve pins, heaters and seals are replaced as wear parts; existing hot runners can also be refurbished.

sections.heading: Cooling design in cap molds
paragraphs: Cooling usually takes the largest share of the injection molding cycle, so cooling layout has a direct effect on output. In a closure mold the core is the hard part to cool, because the heat from the cap interior must be removed through a small-diameter core.
list: Core cooling: a bubbler tube or baffle inside each core brings water close to the cap top and thread area.
Cavity cooling: drilled channels or cooling sleeves around each cavity insert cool the outer shell and top panel.
Flow balance: each cavity should receive the same water flow; restrictions in one branch cause oval or warped caps in those cavities.
Water quality: scale and corrosion reduce flow over time; filtered and treated water keeps cooling performance stable.
Highly conductive insert materials can be used in core tips where extra heat removal is needed.

sections.heading: Wear parts and spare parts for closure molds
paragraphs: Closure molds run at high cycle counts, so a defined spare parts set protects production. LIHE tooling is built to withstand up to 8 million shots on Husky, SACMI and Netstal platforms, and cap mold parts have a lead time of about 4 weeks.
list: Forming parts: core inserts, inner cores, cavity inserts and stripper rings, which wear at the thread, seal and band edges.
Hot runner parts: nozzle tips, valve pins, heaters, thermocouples and seals.
Moving parts: gears, bearings and racks in unscrewing molds; ejector components in stripping molds.
Alignment parts: guide pillars, bushings and taper locks; worn alignment shows as uneven wall thickness or flash.
Consumables: O-rings and cooling seals, replaced at every major service.

sections.heading: Closure mold ordering checklist
steps: Send the cap drawing or cap samples and the matching neck finish drawing (26mm, 28mm, 2925, 3025, 38mm or custom).
State the cap construction, resin grade, cap weight target and whether the band is tamper-evident only or an EU tethered design.
Give the machine model, clamp force, platen and tie-bar dimensions, ejection stroke and any unscrewing drive interface.
Specify cavitation (12 to 72 cavities) and hot runner requirements: valve or open gate, controller type and number of zones.
List cooling water conditions at the mold: available flow, pressure and water treatment.
Agree the spare parts set and the acceptance criteria: sample caps, CMM dimensional reports and a process capability target.
Plan installation and start-up support with the LIHE technical team for the first production run.

sections.heading: Inspection and acceptance of a closure mold
list: Forming parts are measured on an in-house Zeiss CMM; validation and inspection reports are supplied on request.
LIHE tooling consistently achieves CPK ≥ 1.33, a common process capability threshold for critical dimensions.
Cap samples from every cavity are checked for weight spread, thread and seal dimensions and band function.
Operational defect rates as low as 0.0064% have been achieved on LIHE tooling.

faq.question: Why do some cap molds unscrew and others strip the cap off the core?
faq.answer: It depends on the thread and the resin. A shallow, rounded thread in a flexible resin can flex over the core and be stripped off, which keeps the mold simpler. Deeper or sharper threads, or more rigid resins, need rotating cores that unscrew the cap before ejection.

faq.question: How many cavities can a LIHE closure mold hot runner serve?
faq.answer: Closure molds are available from 12 to 72 cavities, and LIHE closure hot runner systems are available for up to 96 cavities.

faq.question: Which closure mold parts should I keep in stock?
faq.answer: Keep core inserts, cavity inserts and stripper rings for the cavities that wear first, plus hot runner nozzle tips, heaters, thermocouples and seals, and O-rings for the cooling circuits. Cap mold parts have a lead time of about 4 weeks, so the stock should cover at least that period.

faq.question: What causes cap weight differences between cavities?
faq.answer: Common causes are an unbalanced or partly blocked hot runner zone, a heater or thermocouple fault, uneven cooling flow between cavities, or worn alignment parts that shift the core. Checking zone temperatures and cooling flow per cavity is the usual starting point.

faq.question: Is the closure mold compatible with my machine?
faq.answer: LIHE closure molds are made for mainstream closure injection molding machines and SACMI compression machines. Send the machine model and interface dimensions with your request so the mold base, ejection and hot runner connection are designed to fit.

product-21.heading: Compression mold replacement tooling for SACMI CCM cap production lines: punches, dies, cores, cooling inserts and wear parts
product-21.intro: Replacement compression tooling refers to the punches, dies, cores, cooling inserts and wear parts that are remade to the same dimensions as the originals so that a SACMI CCM continuous compression molding line can keep running after its tooling wears. This page is a practical reference for maintenance and purchasing teams: which parts wear and how to recognise it, how to send existing parts to LIHE so they can be reproduced, how replacement parts are inspected and how to maintain tooling between replacements. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China.

sections.heading: Why compression tooling needs replacement
paragraphs: A CCM machine carries many identical tooling stations on its carousel, and every station closes once per revolution. Over millions of cycles the forming surfaces, sealing edges and contact faces wear. Because all stations must produce the same cap, one worn station can cause rejects even when the rest of the carousel is in good condition.
list: Typical triggers: cap dimensions drifting out of tolerance, flash at the band or top panel, sticking during extraction, or cooling water leaks.
Replacing a few stations at a time keeps the line running; replacing the whole carousel set is usually planned with a cap design change or neck conversion.
LIHE makes replacement tooling from customers' existing parts, so the new parts match the machine and the current cap without a full redesign.
LIHE tooling is built to withstand up to 8 million shots on Husky, SACMI and Netstal platforms.

sections.heading: Compression tooling parts: what wears and what to look for

head: Part
Where wear appears

sections.heading: How to send existing parts for replacement tooling
steps: Identify the machine: SACMI CCM model, number of molds on the carousel and any modifications made to the tooling.
Select reference parts: send one complete, representative station set (punch, die, core, cooling insert) in the best available condition, plus a worn part if you want the wear pattern assessed.
Add the cap information: cap drawing or samples, neck finish (26mm, 28mm, 2925, 3025, 38mm or custom), cap weight and band type, including EU tethered designs.
Include any drawings or previous inspection reports you hold, and note which dimensions have caused problems in production.
Clean and protect the parts: remove resin residue, dry the water passages, apply rust protection and pack each part separately so forming surfaces cannot touch.
State the quantity needed: number of complete stations, individual parts and spare stock.
Agree the inspection reports and the line trial before production of the full quantity starts.

sections.heading: Inspection of replacement compression tooling
paragraphs: A replacement part is only useful if it is interchangeable with the parts already on the carousel. LIHE checks this with in-house measuring equipment and compares new parts against the customer's reference parts and drawings.
list: Zeiss CMM: dimensional measurement of punches, dies and cores against the reference part and drawing; validation and inspection reports are supplied on request.
3D profile scanner and optical projector: checking of profiles such as thread and band forming edges.
Process capability: LIHE tooling consistently achieves CPK ≥ 1.33.
Cap trial: caps from the new stations are compared with caps from existing stations for weight, dimensions and band function.

sections.heading: Maintenance steps between tooling replacements
steps: Record cycles and rejects per station so that worn stations are identified before they affect the whole lot.
At each planned stop, clean resin residue from punches, dies and cores with non-abrasive methods that do not damage polished surfaces.
Check cooling water flow per station and descale or flush passages where flow has dropped.
Inspect seals and wear parts and replace any that show leaks, cuts or deformation.
Check forming edges at the thread, seal and band for damage, and measure critical dimensions on sample caps.
Protect removed parts against corrosion and store them in individual packaging, labelled by station.
Reorder spare parts early: cap mold parts have a lead time of about 4 weeks.

sections.heading: Spare parts planning for SACMI CCM lines
list: Keep complete spare station sets so that a worn station can be swapped as one unit and checked off-line.
Keep a separate stock of seals and small wear parts, which are replaced more often than forming parts.
Size the spare stock to cover at least the 4-week lead time for cap mold parts, plus transport time.
When a cap design changes, plan the replacement tooling and the change of spare stock together.
Remote troubleshooting, on-site assistance, spare parts supply and mold refurbishment programs are available from the LIHE technical team.

faq.question: Can LIHE make replacement tooling from my existing parts?
faq.answer: Yes. LIHE makes replacement compression tooling from customers' existing parts. Send a representative set of parts and cap samples, and add any drawings you hold.

faq.question: Will the replacement parts be interchangeable with my existing stations?
faq.answer: That is the purpose of measuring against your reference parts. New parts are checked on a Zeiss CMM and in a cap trial against caps from your existing stations; inspection reports are supplied on request.

faq.question: How long does replacement tooling take?
faq.answer: Cap mold parts have a lead time of about 4 weeks. Larger scopes, such as a full carousel set or a neck conversion, are scheduled after the parts and cap information have been reviewed.

faq.question: Can replacement tooling be used to change the cap design?
faq.answer: Yes, a replacement set can include design changes such as a different neck finish, a tamper-evident band change or an EU tethered cap. Describe the change when sending the parts so it is included in the design.

faq.question: Which parts should I replace first?
faq.answer: Start with the stations that produce rejects. Seals and small wear parts are usually replaced most often; punches, dies and cores are replaced when cap dimensions or band function can no longer be held.

product-22.heading: Blow mold set technical reference: mold shells, base molds, neck plates, cooling, venting and bottle development
product-22.intro: A blow mold set is the group of parts that one blowing station needs to form a PET bottle: two mold shells, a base mold and a neck plate, plus conversion parts where the mold must fit a different machine. This reference explains what each part does, how materials, cooling, venting and surface finish are chosen in general terms, and the steps from bottle design to approved trial bottles. Use it when you prepare a new bottle project or check an existing mold set.

sections.heading: Parts of a PET blow mold set and what to check
paragraphs: On a rotary blow molder every station carries its own set, so a machine with many stations needs the same number of identical sets. Each part has a clear job, and each one has typical points to check when a set is received or returned from production.

head: Part
Function
What to check
rows: Form the bottle body, shoulder and label panel; carry cooling or heating channels
Parting line fit, cavity surface, vent slots, cooling connections
Forms the bottle base, the thickest and most stressed area; usually cooled separately
Base profile, centering to the shells, vent holes in base feet
Supports the preform neck and support ring so the finished thread is not deformed
Seat diameter, wear on the contact faces, alignment with the stretch rod
Exchangeable cavity parts inside a fixed outer shell for quick format change
Locating faces, fastening, sealing of cooling passages
Adapt one mold design to the mold carrier of another machine

sections.heading: Blow mold materials in general terms
paragraphs: No single material suits every part. The choice balances heat transfer, wear, corrosion and weight, and it is agreed for each project according to output, filling type and the machine.
list: Aluminium alloys: light and good at conducting heat, so the bottle cools quickly; easy to machine and polish, which makes them a common choice for cavity shells on cold fill molds.
Stainless steels: resist corrosion from cooling water and condensation and keep their surface longer; often used for base molds, high-volume molds and parts that run warm.
Tool steels: hard and wear resistant, used for parts with sliding or clamping contact such as neck plates and locking elements.
Weight matters on quick-change machines: lighter shells are easier for operators to handle during a format change.
Hot fill molds run at elevated temperature for long periods, so material and cavity finish are selected for long-term operation under heat.

sections.heading: Cooling channel design in blow mold shells and base molds
paragraphs: The bottle must be cool and stable before it leaves the mold, so cooling has a direct effect on bottle quality and on how fast the machine can run. Channels are drilled or milled close to the cavity and connected to the machine's water circuit through the mold carrier.
list: Shell cooling follows the cavity shape so the bottle wall cools evenly from shoulder to base.
The base mold has its own circuit because the base holds more material and stays warm longest.
Flow is balanced between all sets on the machine so that every station produces the same bottle.
Clean, treated water keeps the channels free of scale; scale acts as insulation and makes bottle quality drift.
In heat-set molds the same idea is used in reverse: the shells carry hot oil to hold the PET at an elevated temperature.

sections.heading: Venting and surface finish of the blow mold cavity
paragraphs: When the preform expands, the air between the PET and the cavity wall must escape in a very short time. If it cannot, the bottle shows soft details, rounded edges or trapped-air marks. Surface finish and venting are therefore designed together.
list: Vent slots along the parting line let air leave the main body area.
Small vent holes or vent inserts are placed in deep details such as logos, ribs, grip areas and the feet of a petaloid base.
A finely blasted (textured) cavity surface helps air escape and is often used outside the clear label areas.
A polished cavity gives a glossy bottle surface; any scratch or mark on it transfers directly to every bottle.
Matte, frosted or embossed designs are produced by local texturing or engraving of the cavity.
An accurate fit between the two shells and the base mold keeps the parting line on the bottle thin and even.

sections.heading: Bottle development steps: from design to preform matching, mold and trial
paragraphs: A new bottle is developed as a project in which the bottle, the preform and the mold are checked against each other before the full set is built. LIHE's engineering and design center uses CAD/CAM, 3D simulation and flow analysis before production.
steps: Collect the requirements: capacity, target bottle weight, neck finish, filling method, label size, carton or pallet limits and the blow molding machine.
Design the bottle in 3D and calculate the brimful and nominal volume; if only a sample exists, it can be measured to create the drawing.
Match the preform: check stretch ratios, wall thickness and weight so the preform gives even material distribution in the bottle, or propose a new or lightweighted preform.
Build a pilot mold (published lead time 20 days) and blow trial bottles on the customer's machine type.
Test the trial bottles for wall thickness distribution, volume, top load and, for carbonated products, pressure resistance; adjust the design if needed.
Approve the design and produce the full mold set (standard PET molds 8 weeks), with inspection on the in-house Zeiss CMM.
Install the set and support machine start-up, with installation and start-up assistance available from the technical team.

sections.heading: Spare parts, conversion and refurbishment of blow mold sets
list: Replacement parts such as base molds, neck plates and cavity inserts have a published lead time of 4 weeks.
Keeping spare base molds for high-volume bottles prevents one damaged part from stopping a station.
Conversion parts let an existing bottle design run on another machine brand without a new bottle approval.
Lightweighting projects adjust the bottle geometry and base design together with the preform, which can reduce the PET used per bottle.
Mold refurbishment programs restore worn sets; validation and inspection reports are available on request.

faq.question: Why is the base mold a separate part of the blow mold?
faq.answer: The base is the thickest and most stressed area of the bottle, and on most machines the base mold moves separately from the shells. A separate part can have its own cooling circuit, can be changed when only the base design changes, and can be kept as a spare.

faq.question: Can you build a blow mold from a sample bottle without a drawing?
faq.answer: A sample bottle is a useful starting point. Send it together with your requirements and ask LIHE sales to confirm whether the 3D model and drawing can be produced from it; LIHE's QC lab includes a 3D profile scanner and bottle sample inspection equipment. The preform still has to be matched, and trial bottles are checked before the full set is produced.

faq.question: What does preform matching mean?
faq.answer: It means checking that the preform's length, diameter, wall thickness and weight suit the bottle, so that the PET stretches evenly into every part of the cavity. A poorly matched preform causes thin spots, thick bases or haze, even in a well-made mold.

faq.question: Do all blowing stations need identical mold sets?
faq.answer: Yes. Each station produces bottles for the same line, so the cavity, base and venting must be the same in every set. Sets are inspected to the same drawing so bottles from all stations behave the same on the filler and labeller.

faq.question: Can an existing blow mold be changed for a lighter bottle?
faq.answer: Often it can. Lightweighting usually combines a lighter preform with changes to the base and wall geometry. Whether the existing shells can be modified or new cavity inserts are needed depends on the size of the change.

product-23.heading: KHS InnoPET Blomax cold fill PET blow mold: compatible replacement molds for beverage bottle lines — mold carrier fit, still water and CSD
product-23.intro: A KHS cold fill blow mold is a set of mold shells, a base mold and a neck plate machined to the mold carrier of a KHS (formerly SIG) InnoPET Blomax stretch blow molder, for bottles filled at ambient temperature. This guide covers what has to match the Blomax mold carrier, the information to send for a quote, design points for lightweight still water and carbonated soft drink (CSD) bottles, and the steps of a format changeover on a Blomax line.

sections.heading: What a KHS Blomax blow mold must match on the mold carrier
paragraphs: A Blomax mold set only works if it seats, locks and connects exactly like the original KHS parts. The bottle cavity can be new, but the outside of each part follows the machine. Because the InnoPET Blomax series has been built over several machine generations under the SIG and KHS names, the details are confirmed from the machine nameplate and documentation for each project.
list: Mold shell outer geometry and mounting faces, so the shells sit in the shell holders of the mold carrier without shims or modification.
Clamping and locking interface of the mold carrier, so the mold closes and locks under blowing pressure.
Position and type of the cooling water connections, so shells and base mold connect to the machine circuit directly.
Base mold mounting and height, matched to the base unit and its stroke so the base closes against the shells at the right point.
Neck plate seat, matched to the preform support ring and centered on the stretch rod axis.
Number of blowing stations, because every station needs an identical set.

sections.heading: Lightweight still water vs CSD bottles on a KHS Blomax
paragraphs: The same Blomax machine often runs both still water and carbonated products, but the bottles behave differently in use, so the mold design priorities differ.

head: Lightweight still water bottle
CSD bottle
rows: None, or a small pressure from nitrogen dosing
Minimum PET weight while keeping top load and handling strength
Resistance to pressure, creep and base stress cracking
Top load, volume, wall thickness distribution
Burst pressure, volume expansion under pressure, base material distribution
Even wall distribution, ribs and shoulder shape for stiffness
Petaloid base geometry and strong base cooling

sections.heading: Design considerations for lightweight still water bottles
list: Lightweighting starts with the preform: preform lightweighting proposals reduce preform weight by 1g to 2g through neck or wall-thickness optimization, and the bottle geometry is then adjusted to the new preform.
Material must reach the shoulder and the label panel evenly, because thin areas buckle first under top load on the filler and capper.
Horizontal ribs and shoulder shape add stiffness without adding PET, but they must also be easy to vent so they form sharply.
Very light bottles are often filled with nitrogen dosing, which gives a small internal pressure and makes the bottle firmer for stacking and handling.
Common water bottle formats are 330ml, 500ml, 550ml and 1.5L; each format is matched to its own preform.

sections.heading: Design considerations for CSD bottles on KHS machines
list: The petaloid base carries the carbonation pressure; its feet, valleys and center must receive enough oriented material.
The base center stays thicker and less oriented than the wall, so the base mold has its own cooling circuit to cool this area well.
Base geometry and material distribution together decide resistance to stress cracking, so the base is checked on trial bottles before the full set is built.
CSD bottles expand slightly under pressure over their shelf life; the design allows for this so the fill level and label fit stay acceptable.
Cooling channels in shells and base molds keep bottle quality stable at production speed, as listed in the product specification above.

sections.heading: Information to send for a KHS Blomax blow mold quote
list: Machine data: KHS or SIG InnoPET Blomax model and generation from the nameplate, number of blowing stations and the mold carrier type.
Bottle data: drawing or sample, capacity, target weight, product (still water, CSD, juice or dairy) and base type.
Preform data: drawing or sample, weight and neck finish, or a request to match a new preform.
Scope: complete sets of shells, base molds and neck plates for all stations, or spare base molds and replacement parts only.
Photos of the existing mold parts and their markings, which help confirm the carrier interface.
Target dates; published lead times are 20 days for pilot molds, 8 weeks for standard PET molds and 4 weeks for replacement parts.

sections.heading: Changeover steps for a KHS Blomax blow mold set
paragraphs: A format change on a Blomax line replaces the set in every blowing station. Always follow the KHS operating manual for the machine-specific procedure and safety lock-out; the sequence below shows the general order of work.
steps: Prepare the new sets: clean, inspected and numbered for each station, with the matching preforms and the bottle recipe ready.
Empty the machine of preforms and bottles, stop it according to the KHS manual and secure it against restart.
Shut off and drain the cooling water to the molds before disconnecting the hoses or couplings.
Open the mold carriers and remove the shells, base molds and neck plates station by station; if the neck finish changes, change the neck-related parts as well.
Install the new parts, check that each shell and base mold is fully seated and locked, and reconnect the cooling water.
Restore cooling flow and check every connection for leaks before the machine is restarted.
Load the recipe, adjust the oven heating profile to the new preform, and blow the first bottles.
Check bottles from each station for volume, wall thickness, base shape and appearance before releasing the line to production.

faq.question: Can LIHE build molds for older SIG-branded Blomax machines?
faq.answer: The cold fill sets are built for the KHS / SIG InnoPET Blomax series. Send the nameplate data and photos of the existing mold parts so the exact carrier interface of your machine generation is matched.

faq.question: Can a mold for a still water bottle also run CSD?
faq.answer: Usually not. A CSD bottle needs a petaloid base and a material distribution designed for carbonation pressure, while a still water bottle is designed for minimum weight with a flat or champagne-style base. A separate base mold, and often a separate cavity, is needed.

faq.question: Can the same bottle design run on both KHS and Krones machines?
faq.answer: The bottle design can be shared, but each machine needs parts that fit its own mold carrier. LIHE supplies conversion parts or a separate set for each platform.

faq.question: How many mold sets do we need for a KHS Blomax?
faq.answer: One identical set per blowing station, plus spare parts for the parts that wear or get damaged most often, such as base molds. The station count comes from the machine model.

faq.question: Do you supply hot fill molds for KHS machines?
faq.answer: This product is the cold fill set for ambient-filled still water, CSD, juice and dairy. Hot fill requires a heat-set machine and a heat-set mold; see the Hot Fill Blow Mold page and send your machine data so compatibility can be checked.

product-24.heading: Lightweight PET water bottle blow mold design for beverage production lines: base, grip panels, top-load and neck finish
product-24.intro: A blow mold for disposable bottled water is a set of cavity halves and a base insert that stretch-blows a heated PET preform into a single-use still water bottle. This guide explains the design choices that decide how light a water bottle can be and still survive the line and the pallet: base shape, grip panels, top-load strength, neck finish and bottle size. It ends with the development steps from bottle drawing to approved samples.

sections.heading: What makes a lightweight water bottle work
paragraphs: In still water, the bottle carries no internal pressure after capping, so the main loads are vertical: the capper pushing down, stacked cases and pallets, and handling by the consumer. A lightweight bottle works when the PET that remains is placed where these loads act and removed where it does nothing.

Bottle weight is set by the preform, but where the material ends up is set by the blow mold geometry and the stretch ratios between preform and bottle. For that reason the bottle and the preform should be designed as one pair, not ordered separately.
list: Material distribution: aim for even wall thickness in the shoulder, panel and heel; thick spots add weight without adding strength.
Shoulder geometry: a well-shaped shoulder carries most of the top-load from the neck down into the body.
Base geometry: the base must stand flat after filling and resist rocking on conveyors.
Neck finish: the finish is one of the heaviest parts of the preform and is a direct lever on weight.
LIHE lightweighting proposals reduce preform weight by 1g to 2g through neck or wall-thickness optimization, and the blow mold is adjusted to match the new preform.

sections.heading: Water bottle base design: petaloid vs flat and push-up bases
paragraphs: The base is where blow molding is hardest: material stretches least near the gate, and the base must stand stable on fast conveyors. The right base depends on whether the product is still or carbonated.

head: Petaloid base
Flat / push-up (champagne-style) base
rows: Several feet ("petals") around a central gate area
Flat standing ring with a domed push-up in the center
Sparkling water and some nitrogen-dosed still water lines
Most still water and mineral water bottles
More material in the feet and valleys
Can be blown thinner because there is no internal pressure
Thin or stress-cracked feet if material is short
Base roll-out or rocking if the push-up is too shallow

list: Use a flat or push-up base for standard still water unless the line uses nitrogen dosing or the product is carbonated.
Keep the standing ring wide enough to prevent tipping on transfer points and in conveyor accumulation.
Check base clearance with the filler and capper handling parts before freezing the design.

sections.heading: Grip panels, ribs and top-load strength
paragraphs: Top-load is the vertical force a bottle withstands before it buckles. It is tested on empty and filled bottles because both conditions occur on the line: empty bottles meet the capper and filler, filled bottles meet the pallet stack.
list: Horizontal rings and ribs increase hoop stiffness, which helps bottles keep their shape when squeezed, but rings placed too close to the shoulder can lower top-load.
Grip panels give the consumer a place to hold a thin bottle; they should be shallow and smooth so material can flow into them evenly.
Label panels must stay smooth and round enough for the label to apply without wrinkles.
Sharp corners and deep features trap material and leave thin walls next to them; generous radii distribute PET more evenly.
Very light still water bottles are often filled with a small dose of liquid nitrogen so internal pressure adds rigidity; the bottle design must allow for that pressure.
Confirm top-load targets with the filler, capper and pallet pattern you actually use, not with a general figure.

sections.heading: Neck finish choice for water bottles: PCO 1881, 2925 and 2622
paragraphs: The neck finish fixes the closure, the preform weight in the threaded area and the neck handling parts on the blow molder and filler. Changing it later affects the preform mold, the closure supply and the conveyor parts, so it is decided at the start.

head: Neck finish
Nominal size
Typical water use
Points to check
rows: Still and sparkling water; shared with carbonated soft drink lines
Heavier than short water necks; useful when one line runs both still and carbonated products
Still water with short, lightweight closures
Closure supply and capping heads must match the 29 mm finish
Still water where the lightest neck is wanted
Smaller opening; check closure availability and capper tooling

list: Short water necks such as 2925 and 2622 save material in the neck compared with taller finishes.
If the line also runs carbonated drinks, a shared PCO 1881 finish can keep closures and neck parts common.
The preform mold, the blow mold neck area and neck grippers must all match the chosen finish.

sections.heading: Water bottle sizes: 330ml, 500ml, 550ml and 1.5L
list: 330ml: short bottles where base stability and label area matter; often used for events, hotels and multipacks.
500ml: the most common single-serve size; the main target for lightweighting because volumes are high.
550ml: a variant of the 500ml format used in some markets; it may share the preform with 500ml if the stretch ratios allow it.
1.5L: larger panels and longer bodies need more attention to top-load and paneling; grip areas help the consumer pour.
Producing several sizes from one preform reduces preform mold investment but must be checked for correct stretch ratios in each bottle.
LIHE supplies water bottle blow molds in these sizes for two-step machines (SIDEL, KRONES, SIG/KHS, TECH-LONG, NEWAMSTAR) and one-step machines (SIPA, ASB, AOKI).

sections.heading: Development steps for a new lightweight water bottle blow mold
steps: Define the product: size (for example 500ml), still or carbonated, nitrogen dosing, target bottle weight, closure and neck finish.
Collect line data: blow molding machine model, mold carrier type, filler and capper handling parts, label size and pallet pattern.
Draw the bottle and preform together; LIHE's engineering center uses CAD/CAM, 3D simulation and flow analysis before production.
Review the drawing with the bottler: shape, base, grip panels, label panel and brand features.
Machine the blow mold and, where needed, a matching preform or neck parts.
Blow sample bottles and inspect them: wall thickness distribution, volume, base shape and dimensions; LIHE checks samples with a 3D profile scanner and bottle sample inspection.
Test top-load and stability with the bottler's own filling and capping conditions, adjust the design if needed, and approve for production.

sections.heading: What to send when requesting a water bottle blow mold quote
list: Bottle drawing or sample, or a sketch with size, height and diameter limits.
Preform drawing or sample, including the neck finish (PCO 1881, 2925, 2622 or other).
Machine brand and model, number of cavities and mold carrier type.
Target bottle weight, and whether the project is a new bottle or a lighter version of an existing one.
Filling type (still, sparkling, nitrogen dosed) and any label or pallet constraints.

faq.question: Can an existing water bottle be made lighter without changing the filler?
faq.answer: Often yes. Lightweighting usually changes the preform weight and the blow mold geometry while keeping the neck finish and the outer dimensions that the filler, capper and labeler handle. LIHE lightweighting proposals reduce preform weight by 1g to 2g through neck or wall-thickness optimization.

faq.question: Which base is better for still water, petaloid or flat?
faq.answer: For non-pressurized still water a flat or push-up base is usually enough and uses less material. A petaloid base is designed to resist internal pressure, so it is used for sparkling water and some nitrogen-dosed still water bottles.

faq.question: Should I choose PCO 1881 or a short water neck like 2925 or 2622?
faq.answer: Short water necks save material and suit lines that only run still water. PCO 1881 is a common choice when the same line also fills carbonated drinks, because closures and neck handling parts can be shared.

faq.question: Can 500ml and 550ml bottles use the same preform?
faq.answer: Sometimes. It depends on the stretch ratios between the preform and each bottle. The bottle and preform drawings should be checked together before deciding to share one preform.

faq.question: Which blow molding machines are these molds made for?
faq.answer: Two-step machines such as SIDEL, KRONES, SIG/KHS, TECH-LONG and NEWAMSTAR, and one-step machines such as SIPA, ASB and AOKI. The machine model and mold carrier type are needed with the request.

product-25.heading: Blow mold changeover cost for PET bottle lines: when a split-type quick-change system pays off vs full mold sets
product-25.intro: A split-type quick-change blow mold is a blow mold in which the bottle-shaped cavity inserts and the base are separate from mold shells that stay mounted in the machine, so a format change replaces only the inserts. This guide looks at the full cost of changeovers on a rotary blow molder and shows when a split-type system pays off compared with buying a complete mold set for every bottle. It also gives a changeover procedure and a method for planning SKUs around shared shells.

sections.heading: What a blow mold changeover really costs
paragraphs: The price of a mold set is only one part of the cost of running many bottle formats. Each format change also stops the line and consumes labor and material. These costs repeat every time the format changes, so they grow with the number of SKUs and the frequency of changes.
list: Line downtime: the blow molder, and usually the filler behind it, produce nothing while molds are changed and the new format is started.
Labor: technicians for mold removal, installation, adjustment and first-bottle checks, often with a crane or lifting device for full mold sets.
Start-up scrap: preforms and bottles rejected while the heating profile and blowing conditions are tuned for the new shape.
Tooling investment: a complete mold set per cavity for every bottle shape, or one set of shells plus inserts for each shape.
Storage and handling: full mold sets are heavier and take more storage space, protection and handling equipment than inserts.
Wear and damage risk: frequent removal and remounting of heavy parts increases the chance of damaged cooling connections and locating surfaces.

sections.heading: Full mold set vs split-type quick-change blow mold: comparison

head: Full mold set per format
Split-type quick-change mold
rows: Complete mold halves, shells and base for every cavity
Cavity inserts and base only; shells stay in the mold carrier
Tooling for a new bottle shape

sections.heading: When a split-type quick-change blow mold pays off
paragraphs: A split-type system makes sense when the savings from shorter changeovers and cheaper new shapes are larger than the cost of the shells and the engineering needed to fit several bottles into one shell family.
list: The line runs many SKUs in one size family, for example several 500ml shapes for different brands or customers.
Formats change weekly or more often, so downtime per changeover is multiplied many times per year.
New bottle shapes are launched regularly, such as seasonal or promotional packaging.
Bottles share the same neck finish and preform, so the heating and stretch settings change little between formats.
A full set still makes sense when a line runs one or two formats for months at a time, or when the new bottle is so different in diameter or height that it cannot fit the existing shell.

sections.heading: Estimating annual changeover cost: a simple worksheet
paragraphs: Use your own line data. The figures below only show how to set up the calculation; they are not performance data for any specific mold.
list: Changeovers per year = changeovers per week × operating weeks. Example: 3 changeovers per week × 52 weeks = 156 changeovers per year.
Downtime per year = changeovers per year × hours per changeover (measured from last good bottle to first good bottle).
Lost output = downtime per year × line output per hour.
Start-up scrap = changeovers per year × preforms rejected per start-up.
Tooling = (number of new shapes per year × cost of a full set) compared with (shells once + number of new shapes × cost of inserts and base).
Compare the totals over the expected life of the shells; the difference is the value of moving to a split-type system.
Track changeover time as part of overall equipment effectiveness (OEE), where it appears as availability loss.

sections.heading: Quick-change blow mold changeover procedure
paragraphs: SMED (single-minute exchange of die) is a lean method that aims to bring tool changes under 10 minutes by separating work done while the machine runs (external) from work done while it is stopped (internal). The steps below apply that idea to a split-type blow mold.
steps: Before stopping the line, prepare the next format: inserts and bases cleaned, checked and labeled by cavity, tools and the machine recipe ready.
Run out the current format and stop the blow molder according to its safety procedure.
Open the mold stations and release the inserts and base from the shells, leaving the shells in the mold carrier.
Install the new inserts and base in each station and lock them, checking that each part is seated correctly.
If the preform changes, change the preform-related parts and settings as well, such as the stretch rod stroke and oven heating profile.
Load the new machine recipe, start at reduced output and check the first bottles for volume, wall distribution, base shape and dimensions.
Release to full speed, then record the changeover time and any problems so the next change can be shorter.

sections.heading: SKU planning around shared shells
list: Group bottles into size families that fit one shell envelope, for example 500ml and 550ml shapes with similar diameter and height.
Keep the same neck finish and, where possible, the same preform within a family so only the inserts and base change.
Sequence production so that formats from the same family run back to back, and changes between families are planned for scheduled stops.
Keep one spare set of inserts and bases for the highest-volume shapes so worn parts can be replaced without stopping production.
Design new SKUs to fit an existing shell family whenever the marketing brief allows it; this keeps tooling to inserts only.
Document every insert set by cavity number and format, and store them in protective racks near the machine.

sections.heading: What LIHE needs to quote a split-type quick-change mold
list: Blow molding machine brand, model and mold carrier type; LIHE builds blow molds for SIDEL, KRONES, SIG/KHS, TECH-LONG and NEWAMSTAR two-step machines and SIPA, ASB and AOKI one-step machines.
Drawings or samples of all bottles to run in the shell family, with their preforms and neck finishes.
Expected number of formats and how often they change.
Whether existing shells are to be reused, with their drawings or condition, or new shells are needed.
Any related accessories such as stretch rods, blowing pins or neck grippers for formats with different preforms.

faq.question: Can any new bottle shape use the existing shells?
faq.answer: Only if it fits the shell envelope, mainly the maximum diameter and height, and uses a compatible neck and base arrangement. Bottles that are much larger or smaller usually need their own shells or a full mold set.

faq.question: How much changeover time does a split-type mold save?
faq.answer: It depends on the machine, the number of cavities and how the changeover is organized. Measure your current time from last good bottle to first good bottle, then compare it with a trial changeover of inserts only. Good preparation of external tasks often matters as much as the mold design.

faq.question: Do I still need to change parts other than the inserts?
faq.answer: If the new format uses the same preform and neck finish, usually only the inserts and base change. If the preform or neck changes, preform-related parts such as stretch rods and neck handling parts, and the machine settings, also change.

faq.question: Is a split-type mold suitable for hot fill bottles?
faq.answer: Hot fill bottles, filled at about 85–95°C, need heat-set molds with heated mold surfaces because standard PET deforms above about 60°C. Whether a quick-change insert design suits a specific hot fill bottle and machine has to be checked case by case.

faq.question: Which machines can use LIHE split-type quick-change molds?
faq.answer: They are adapted to the quick-change mold carriers of mainstream rotary blow molding machines. Send the machine brand, model and carrier type so the shell interface can be confirmed.

product-26.heading: Krones Contiform cold fill PET blow mold: compatible replacement molds, quick-change locking and changeover for beverage bottle lines

This guide focuses on the Contiform interface: how manual and tool-free quick-change carriers affect the mold, what to send for a quote, how to plan sets and spares for frequent format changes, and the steps of a quick changeover.

sections.heading: The Contiform mold carrier: what the blow mold must fit
paragraphs: On a Contiform, each blowing station has a mold carrier that opens and closes the shells, holds the base mold and connects the mold to the machine's cooling circuit. A replacement mold is accepted by the machine only when its outside matches the carrier exactly; the bottle cavity inside can be a new design.
list: Shell back faces and locating features, so the shells sit in the carrier in the same position as the original parts.
Locking features for the carrier's quick-change system, whether the shells are fixed with fasteners or with tool-free locking elements.
Cooling connections in the positions the carrier expects, so the water circuit connects without adapters.
Base mold fit to the base unit, including its locating diameter and height, so the base closes against the shells correctly.
Neck plate seat for the preform support ring, centered on the stretch rod.
Machine model and generation, read from the nameplate, because carrier details can differ between Contiform versions.

sections.heading: Manual vs tool-free quick-change mold carriers on Krones Contiform
paragraphs: LIHE's Contiform sets are compatible with both manual and tool-free quick-change mold carriers. The two systems ask different things of the mold, so the carrier type must be known before design starts.

sections.heading: Why quick-change compatibility matters for the blow mold design
list: Locating features on the shells must be machined to tight tolerances, because the carrier relies on them instead of manual alignment.
Shell weight affects how easily an operator handles parts during a fast change, so material and wall sections are chosen with handling in mind.
Base molds must center themselves on the base unit, so a quick change does not need adjustment of the base position.
Identical outer dimensions across all sets mean any set can go into any station without sorting or shimming.

sections.heading: Planning sets and spare parts for frequent format changes
paragraphs: Contiform lines that run several products often switch between bottle sizes such as 330ml, 500ml, 550ml and 1.5L. Planning the mold sets as a system makes these changes predictable.
list: One identical set per blowing station for each bottle format, so the full machine can run every format.
Spare base molds and neck plates for the formats that run most, because these parts see the most handling during changes.
A labelled storage rack or trolley per format, so a complete set can be moved to the machine at once.
Common neck plates across formats with the same neck finish, which reduces the number of parts touched in a change.

list: Machine: Krones Contiform model and generation from the nameplate, number of blowing stations, and carrier type (manual or tool-free quick-change).
Bottle: drawing or sample, capacity, target weight, product (still water, CSD, juice or another ambient-filled beverage) and base type.
Preform: drawing or sample, weight and neck finish, or a request to design a matched preform.
Existing parts: photos of a current shell, base mold and neck plate with their markings, which help confirm the carrier interface.
Scope: complete sets for all stations, split-type quick-change inserts, or spare parts only.

sections.heading: Quick changeover steps for a Krones Contiform mold set
paragraphs: Follow the Krones operating manual for machine-specific procedures and safety; the sequence below shows how to organize a quick change so the machine is stopped for as little time as possible.
steps: Before the stop, stage the new sets by station number next to the machine, with the preforms, recipe and any neck-related change parts ready.
Run the machine empty of preforms and bottles, stop it according to the Krones manual and secure it against restart.
Shut off the mold cooling water and release the pressure in the circuit.
Open each carrier, release the manual fasteners or the tool-free locking elements, and remove shells, base mold and neck plate.
Fit the new parts, engage the locking elements or tighten the fasteners, and check that every part is fully seated.
Restore cooling water and check each station for leaks.
Load the recipe and adjust the oven heating profile for the new preform.
Blow sample bottles and check each station for volume, wall distribution, base shape and appearance before releasing production.
Clean, check and store the removed sets on their own rack so they are ready for the next change.

faq.question: Are LIHE Contiform molds compatible with tool-free quick-change carriers?
faq.answer: Yes. The cold fill sets are built for Contiform manual and tool-free quick-change mold carriers. Tell us which type your machine has so the locking and locating features are machined for it.

faq.question: Can I mix LIHE sets and original sets on the same machine?
faq.answer: Sets are built to fit the same carrier interface, but all stations should run the same bottle design so bottles are identical. For a new bottle design, supply sets for every station; for an existing design, replacement parts can be built to your current drawing or sample.

faq.question: What should we stock as spare parts for a Contiform line?
faq.answer: Base molds and neck plates for the highest-volume formats are the usual priority, because they see the most handling and wear. Replacement parts have a published lead time of 4 weeks.

faq.question: Can a Contiform mold be converted to run on a KHS machine?
faq.answer: The bottle design can be reused, but the parts must fit the KHS mold carrier. LIHE supplies conversion parts or builds a separate set for the KHS InnoPET Blomax platform.

faq.question: Is a split-type quick-change mold worth it on a Contiform?
faq.answer: It is most useful when the line changes formats often: only cavity inserts and base molds are exchanged, so fewer and lighter parts are handled at each station. For lines with few format changes, complete sets are usually simpler.

product-27.heading: Hot runner system for PET preform molds: cavitation, compatible Husky and Netstal replacement, spare parts, refurbishment and troubleshooting

This page is a working reference for buyers and maintenance teams: what the LIHE hot runner covers, which spare parts to stock, when to refurbish and how to troubleshoot common hot runner faults. Valve pins — the pin tip seals the gate every cycle; wear or damage shows as gate defects in a specific cavity.
Heaters — manifold and nozzle heaters can fail open-circuit or lose output with age.

sections.heading: Hot runner refurbishment: what is usually done
paragraphs: Refurbishment returns a used hot runner to stable production condition. LIHE refurbishes existing hot runners and, more broadly, offers mold refurbishment programs and project retrofitting to restore aging assets to OEM-level efficiency. sections.heading: Troubleshooting a hot runner: step-by-step procedure
steps: Identify the affected cavities and note the symptom: short shot, heavy or light preform, gate defect, stringing or leak.

Check valve pin operation: actuation pressure, timing and whether the pin closes fully in the affected cavity.
Inspect the gate insert and nozzle tip area of the affected cavity for damage, wear or contamination.
Replace the faulty part (tip, pin, heater or seal) and confirm by weighing preforms from the affected and neighboring cavities.
If several zones fail or leaks appear, plan a full refurbishment and contact LIHE for remote troubleshooting or on-site assistance.

product-28.heading: Blowing pin and stretch rod wear: inspection, replacement planning and neck finish matching
product-28.intro: A stretch rod is a precision rod that pushes the heated PET preform down to the base of the blow mold before and during blowing, while the blowing pin (blowing nozzle) seals the preform neck and delivers the blowing air. Both parts work in every cycle, so they wear gradually and the first warning signs usually appear in the bottles and in air consumption, not in the parts themselves. This guide explains how to recognise wear, how to inspect blowing pins and stretch rods, and how to plan replacement parts so a stretch blow molding machine keeps producing consistent bottles.

sections.heading: How blowing pins and stretch rods wear in a stretch blow molding machine
paragraphs: In two-step stretch blow molding, the blowing pin moves down onto the preform neck in every cycle, and the stretch rod travels through the neck and along the full preform length. Wear comes from this repeated contact and movement, not from a single event.
list: Sealing faces and seals on the blowing pin flatten, scratch or harden, so the seal against the preform neck finish becomes less reliable.
Guide bushings around the stretch rod wear oval, which lets the rod move sideways instead of running straight down the preform axis.
The stretch rod itself can bend after a preform misfeed or a collision, and its surface can be scored by dirt or worn guides.
The stretch rod tip is the part that touches the hot preform base; a damaged or worn tip leaves marks on the bottle base and can shift the gate off center.
O-rings and dynamic seals in the blowing head lose elasticity over time, especially in stations that run hot or are cleaned with aggressive agents.

sections.heading: Signs of wear: air leaks, off-center stretching and bottle defects
paragraphs: Most wear problems show up first as bottle defects that appear in one blowing station and not in the others. Sorting rejects by station number is the fastest way to find the worn part.
list: Air leaks: an audible hiss at the nozzle during blowing, higher compressed-air consumption, or bottles that are not fully formed at the shoulder, base or corners.
Off-center stretching: the injection point (gate) is not in the center of the bottle base, wall thickness differs from one side of the bottle to the other, or bottles lean.
Base defects: pinholes or blow-outs at the gate, rod-tip marks, thin or unstable petaloid feet.
Neck finish damage: scratches, dents or ovality on the top sealing surface of the neck, which can later cause cap leaks.
Station-specific rejects: defects that follow one blowing station even after the blow mold has been cleaned point to the blowing pin or stretch rod of that station.

sections.heading: Inspection steps for blowing pins and stretch rods
steps: Stop the machine, follow the lockout procedure and vent the compressed-air system before touching the blowing head.
Record which stations produce rejects and keep sample bottles from each station for comparison.
Remove the blowing pin and inspect the sealing face and seals under good light for flattening, cuts, cracks and hardening.
Check the stretch rod for straightness by rolling it on V-blocks with a dial indicator, and look for scoring along its length.
Inspect the stretch rod tip for wear, chips and PET residue, and compare its profile with a new part or the drawing.
Check play between the stretch rod and its guide bushing; any noticeable side movement means the bushing should be replaced.
Measure critical diameters against the drawing or a reference part and record the results per station.
Reassemble, check alignment of the nozzle to the mold neck area, then run a short trial and inspect the gate position and neck surface on the bottles.

sections.heading: Replacement planning for blowing pins and stretch rods
list: Keep at least one complete spare set (blowing pin, stretch rod, tip, seals) for the most used format, so a worn station can be changed during a short stop.
Replace seals and O-rings as consumables at planned maintenance stops, instead of waiting for leaks.
Keep a station log of inspections and part changes; patterns in the log show which parts reach end of life first on your line.
Order replacement parts before stock runs out: LIHE's stated lead time for replacement parts is 4 weeks.
LIHE makes blowing pins and stretch rods from customers' existing parts or drawings for SIDEL, KRONES, KHS and other blow molding machines, so send a sample part or drawing with the order.
When a new bottle format is planned, order the blowing pins and stretch rods together with the blow mold as one conversion package.

sections.heading: Neck finish matching: PCO 1881, 38mm and other finishes
paragraphs: The blowing pin must seal on the correct surface of the preform neck finish. Two neck finishes can look similar but differ in sealing surface diameter, neck height and inner diameter, so a nozzle made for one finish may leak or damage another.
list: A neck finish conversion, for example from PCO 1810 to PCO 1881 or to a 38mm finish, usually requires new or modified blowing pins.
The stretch rod diameter must leave enough clearance to the preform inner diameter, and the rod stroke must suit the preform length and bottle height.
Wide-mouth finishes such as 45mm, 68mm or 90mm need nozzles sized for the larger sealing diameter.
Send the preform drawing, neck finish drawing and bottle drawing so the nozzle, rod and tip can be matched to all three.

faq.question: How do I know if a blowing pin is leaking?
faq.answer: Typical signs are a hissing sound at the nozzle during blowing, rising compressed-air consumption and bottles that are not fully formed at the shoulder or base. If the problem stays with one station, inspect that station's blowing pin seal and sealing face first.

faq.question: What causes the gate to be off center in the bottle base?
faq.answer: The most common causes are a bent stretch rod, a worn guide bushing that lets the rod move sideways, or a worn rod tip. Uneven preform heating can produce a similar defect, so check the rod and bushing first and then review the heating profile.

faq.question: Can stretch rods be repaired or must they be replaced?
faq.answer: A rod with minor tip marks can sometimes be polished, but a bent or deeply scored rod should be replaced, because straightening rarely restores the original accuracy. Worn guide bushings are normally replaced, not repaired.

faq.question: Do I need new blowing pins when I change the neck finish?
faq.answer: Usually yes. The nozzle seals on the neck finish, and the sealing diameter and neck height change between finishes such as PCO 1810, PCO 1881 and 38mm. Check the nozzle against the new neck finish drawing before production.

faq.question: What should I send to order replacement blowing pins and stretch rods?
faq.answer: Send the machine make and model, an existing part or its drawing, and the preform and bottle drawings. LIHE makes these parts from customers' existing parts or drawings and states a lead time of 4 weeks for replacement parts.

sections.heading: Plate stack checklist for a preform mold base specification
paragraphs: A preform mold base consists of a hot half and a cold half. For each plate in the order, the specification should state the following, either on the drawing or in a separate list.
list: Plate name and position in the stack: manifold plate, backing plate, cavity plate, core plate, stripper plate or slide plates.

sections.heading: Mold base materials and surface treatments in general terms
paragraphs: Material and treatment choices depend on the plate's function, the mold's expected service life and the cooling water quality in your plant. The points below describe common practice in mold making; the material for your order is agreed during the quotation and shown on the drawing.
list: Pre-hardened mold steels are widely used for plates because they can be machined to final size without a hardening step that could distort the plate.
Stainless mold steels are often chosen for plates with many cooling channels, because they resist corrosion from cooling water and keep channel cross-sections open.
Hardened tool steels are used for wear parts such as guide bushings, taper locks and inserts that slide or lock against each other.
Surface treatments such as nitriding increase surface hardness on wear areas; corrosion-protection coatings are used on surfaces exposed to moisture.
If your plant already runs molds of the same type, state the materials used in them, so new and existing plates behave alike in maintenance.

sections.heading: Inspection on Zeiss CMM: what is measured before delivery
paragraphs: Plates are machined on Mazak, Makino and Haas CNC centers and ground on Okamoto precision grinders. Before delivery, flatness, parallelism and cavity-position accuracy are verified on the in-house Zeiss CMM, and validation and inspection reports are supplied on request.
list: Flatness of the main faces and parallelism between them.
Position of every cavity and core bore relative to the datum, which matters most on 72-cavity to 160-cavity layouts.
Diameters of guide, locating and cavity bores.
Positions of cooling channel entries and connection points.
On request, a report that lists nominal values, tolerances and measured values, which you can keep as a baseline for later wear checks.

sections.heading: Built to your drawing vs designed in-house by LIHE
paragraphs: Mold bases are manufactured to customer drawings or designed in-house for new molds. The choice affects what you send and who is responsible for the design.

product-31.heading: Hot fill blow mold operation and maintenance: hot oil circuits, temperature zones, vacuum panels and bottle defects
product-31.intro: A hot fill (heat-set) blow mold is a PET blow mold whose shells are heated by circulating hot oil so that the bottle is crystallized and stress-relieved during blowing and can be filled at about 85–95°C. Standard PET bottles deform above about 60°C, so the mold's temperature control, the bottle's vacuum panels and the filling conditions must work together. This guide covers how the hot oil circuits and temperature zones are run, how vacuum panels are designed, start-up and shutdown practice, the common hot fill bottle defects with what to check, and routine maintenance.

sections.heading: Hot oil circuits in a heat-set blow mold
paragraphs: In a cold fill mold, water removes heat from the bottle as fast as possible. In a heat-set mold the shells are deliberately held hot, so the PET stays at an elevated temperature against the cavity wall long enough to crystallize and relax the stress from stretching. A heat transfer oil is used because it can carry heat at mold temperatures where water would need a pressurized system.
list: A temperature control unit on the machine heats the oil and pumps it through channels in each mold shell.
Channels run close to the cavity and follow its shape, so the whole bottle wall reaches the same heat-set condition.
Hoses, couplings and seals in the circuit must be rated for hot oil; ordinary water hoses and seals are not suitable.
Thermal insulation between the hot shells and the mold carrier limits heat flow into the machine.
All stations are supplied from the same system and must reach the same temperature, otherwise bottles from different stations behave differently on the filler.
The machine itself must be a heat-set version; LIHE builds hot fill molds for heat-set versions of mainstream two-step rotary blowers, including SIDEL and KRONES.

sections.heading: Body and base temperature zones in a hot fill blow mold
paragraphs: The body and the base of a hot fill bottle need different treatment, so the mold has separate temperature control of body and base. Actual set points are given by the machine maker and fine-tuned on trial bottles; the table shows what each zone does.

head: Zone
Role in the heat-set process

rows: Held hot by oil to crystallize and stabilize the sidewall, shoulder and vacuum panels

sections.heading: Vacuum panel design for hot fill PET bottles
paragraphs: After capping, the hot product and the headspace cool and contract, which creates a vacuum inside the bottle. Vacuum panels are areas designed to move inward in a controlled way so the rest of the bottle keeps its shape. The panels are formed by the shape of the mold cavity, so their design is part of the mold design.
list: Panels are usually placed in the label area, where the label covers their movement and supports the bottle.
Panels are spaced evenly around the bottle so it pulls in symmetrically and does not become oval.
Ribs and frames around the panels keep the shoulder and base rigid while the panels flex.
Some designs let the base take part of the vacuum, which reduces the panel area needed in the sidewall.
Panel edges and ribs need good venting in the mold so they form sharply; soft edges change how the panel flexes.
Square and round hot fill bottles both use this principle; the panel layout follows the bottle cross-section.

sections.heading: Start-up and shutdown of a hot fill blow mold
steps: Before start-up, inspect hot oil hoses, couplings and seals on every station and check the oil level in the temperature control unit.
Heat the molds to the set points for body and base and wait until every station is stable at temperature before blowing.
Blow the first bottles and check appearance, base shape and wall distribution from each station.
Run a hot fill test on sample bottles at the actual filling temperature of the line, cap and cool them, then measure volume and check panel and base movement.
Release production only when bottles from all stations pass the hot fill test.
At shutdown, stop the preform feed first and keep oil circulating while the molds cool down under the control unit's program.
Disconnect hot oil couplings only when the mold is cool enough to handle, and cap them to keep out dirt and moisture.

sections.heading: Maintenance checklist for heat-set blow molds
list: Check hot oil couplings and seals for leaks at every shift; oil on the cavity or parting line marks bottles and is a burn and fire risk.
Replace hoses and seals that are hard, cracked or swollen, and follow the temperature control unit maker's schedule for oil condition.
Inspect thermal insulation between the shells and the mold carrier and replace damaged insulation.
Clean vent slots and holes, especially around vacuum panels and base features.
Check parting line faces and locating features for wear, because heating and cooling cycles add stress to these areas.
Clean and protect cavity surfaces according to their finish; the material and cavity finish are chosen for long-term operation at elevated temperature.
Keep spare base molds and seals for high-volume formats; replacement parts have a published lead time of 4 weeks, and mold refurbishment programs are available.

faq.question: Can a cold fill blow mold be converted to hot fill?
faq.answer: Generally not. A heat-set mold needs hot oil channels, separate body and base temperature control, insulation from the carrier and a bottle design with vacuum panels, and it must run on a heat-set version of the blow molder. In most cases a new mold set is designed for hot fill.

faq.question: What filling temperature should we give when ordering?
faq.answer: Give the actual filling temperature and its tolerance on your line, the product and the cooling method after filling. Hot fill molds are designed for products filled at about 85–95°C, and the design is checked with a hot fill test at your real conditions.

faq.question: Why do hot fill bottles need vacuum panels?
faq.answer: When the hot product cools in the closed bottle, it contracts and creates a vacuum. Without designed panels the bottle would collapse or distort in random places. Panels move inward in a controlled way so the bottle keeps its shape and label area.

faq.question: Can hot fill bottles be lightweighted like water bottles?
faq.answer: Within limits. The heat-set structure, panels and ribs need enough material to stay stable after filling, so weight reduction is checked carefully with hot fill tests on trial bottles. Preform and bottle design are adjusted together.

faq.question: Which blow molding machines do your hot fill molds fit?
faq.answer: Heat-set versions of mainstream two-step rotary blowers, including SIDEL and KRONES. Send the machine model and generation so the mold fits the carrier and the hot oil connections.

product-34.heading: PET preform mold conversion guide: replacement parts, neck finish conversion, lightweight preforms and cooling upgrades
product-34.intro: A tooling conversion is a project that changes or renews the stack parts of an existing PET preform mold — instead of buying a complete new mold — to replace worn parts, change the neck finish, reduce preform weight or shorten the cycle. This guide sorts conversion work into four project types and lists what is needed for each, so a plant can prepare the right data before asking for a quotation. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China.

Conversion parts are 100% interchangeable for Husky, SACMI, SIPA, NETSTAL, MHT, OTTO, ASB, Krupps and Corvaglia systems.

paragraphs: A neck finish conversion changes the threaded top of the preform so the bottle can use a different closure. Because the neck is formed by the neck rings and the top of the core, these parts are always replaced; the cavity and cavity-side parts may also change if the preform body changes. LIHE supports special neck finishes such as PCO 1881 and 29/25 as well as production line conversions.
A neck change also affects equipment outside the mold. Blow molders and conveyors handle bottles by the neck, so neck grippers, guides and star wheels may need new parts as well.

sections.heading: Lightweight preform conversion and rPET
paragraphs: Lightweighting removes resin from the preform while keeping the bottle within its performance limits. LIHE lightweighting proposals reduce preform weight by 1g to 2g through neck or wall-thickness optimization. Retrofitting an existing mold for lightweighting costs only 25%–40% of a new mold price, with a short payback period because resin savings start with the first production run.

Lighter preforms change how the bottle blows, so the project should include blow trials on the customer's blow molder. When the plant is moving to recycled PET, LIHE can include rPET material trials in the same project.
list: Bottle drawing and current preform drawing with actual weight.
Performance targets for the bottle, such as top load, burst or filling conditions.
Blow molder model and current blowing parameters.
Resin grade and planned rPET content.

sections.heading: Cooling upgrade to shorten preform cycle time
paragraphs: A cooling upgrade redesigns how heat leaves the stack — typically around the neck, which is the thickest part of the preform. LIHE optimizes cooling efficiency and blowing conditions to shorten cycle times; optimized cooling can reduce neck cooling time by up to 0.5 seconds. The resulting cycle depends on the full system, so LIHE does not quote cycle times without the customer's data.

Cooling water temperature, flow and water treatment at the mold.
Defects that appear when the cycle is shortened (for example ovality or gate marks).
Machine model and post-mold cooling layout.

sections.heading: Conversion or new mold: how to decide

product-38.heading: Blow mold shell systems for quick change: shells vs cavity inserts, cooling and when to buy complete molds
product-38.intro: A mold shell system is a two-level blow mold design in which a permanent shell (shell holder) stays mounted in the machine's mold carrier and only the bottle-shaped cavity inserts are exchanged when the format changes. The shell takes over the machine interface and cooling distribution, while the insert carries the bottle shape. This guide explains how the work is divided between shells and inserts, what to check on the cooling connections, and how to decide between buying shells with inserts or complete blow molds.

sections.heading: How a shell-type quick-change blow mold divides the work
paragraphs: In a conventional blow mold, each mold half is one solid block that contains both the bottle cavity and all mounting and cooling features. A shell system splits these functions into two parts.
list: Mold shell: mounts in the mold carrier or on the clamping base, holds the cavity half in position, and distributes cooling water from the machine to the insert.
Cavity insert: carries the bottle shape, the surface finish, vent details and any embossing or label panel. It is the part that changes with the bottle design.
Base mold: forms the bottle base (for example a petaloid base for carbonated drinks) and usually changes with the bottle as well.
Locating features between shell and insert decide repeatability: the insert must return to the same position after every change.
Because only inserts and base molds change, a new bottle format needs less machined material and fewer heavy parts are lifted during the changeover.

sections.heading: Cooling connections in mold shells
paragraphs: The bottle is cooled by contact with the cavity, so mold temperature control directly affects bottle shape, shrinkage and cycle stability. In a shell system, the heat has to pass from the insert through the shell contact surface into the cooling water.
list: Drilled channels in the shell carry water close to the insert; their layout must match the machine's water connections.
Insert-to-shell contact surfaces must be clean and flat; dirt or scale on these faces reduces heat transfer.
Where water passes from shell to insert, O-rings or seals are used; damaged seals cause leaks and lower flow in that mold half.
Aluminum alloy shells are lightweight and have high thermal conductivity, which supports even mold temperature.

Hot fill bottles (filled at about 85–95°C, while standard PET deforms above about 60°C) use heat-set molds with a different temperature control design, so the fill type must be known before shells are specified.
After every change, pressure-check the circuit and confirm flow in both halves before production.
